title: ‘Cuse Coats for Community
description:
This November, Syracuse University is inviting faculty, staff and students to help keep Central New York neighbors warm this winter through ‘Cuse Coats for Community. From Monday, Nov. 16 through Friday, Nov. 20 the campus community can drop off new or gently used coats at collection bins across campus. All donated coats will go directly to InterFaith Works to be distributed to community members in need. Children’s coats are needed most, though InterFaith Works is happy to accept coats of all sizes.

Collection bins will be available at the following locations: 

  • Hendricks Chapel near People’s Place Café
  • Bird Library on the first floor by the stairs facing Waverly Avenue
  • The Nancy Cantor Warehouse on the first floor by the DPS office
  • 610 Skytop Road in the Human Resources lobby area
  • The National Veterans Resource Center on the bottom floor by the Gallery
  • Sims Hall in the Department of Public Safety lobby
  • Crouse-Hinds Hall on the first floor behind the front desk

Those who don’t have a coat to give or who would like to support the drive in another way can contribute through an Amazon Wishlist set up by InterFaith Works. Items ordered from the list are delivered directly to InterFaith Works.

title: Biblio Gallery Exhibit: Celia: A Story that Persists
description:
The new Biblio Gallery exhibit on the 4th floor of Bird Library was curated by Juliana Acosta Gil G'27 (College of Arts and Sciences). 

Elena Fortún (Madrid, 1886 – Madrid, 1953) seudónimo de Encarnación Aragoneses Urquijo y la creadora de la zaga Celia. Sus historias acompañaron a niñas y niños y dieron espacio a una voz infantil curiosa, imaginativa y llena de preguntas. Celia nació en las páginas de Elena Fortún durante un momento de grandes cambios en España.

La Guerra Civil (1936–1939) transformó la vida de muchas personas. Elena Fortún se exilió en Argentina, donde continuó escribiendo. Después de la guerra, comenzó una nueva etapa en España. Bajo la dictadura franquista, las publicaciones podían ser revisadas y sometidas a censura.

¿Qué es la censura?

Es el control sobre lo que puede publicarse, circular o llegar a los lectores.

Abre el libro. Lee. Escucha a Celia.

Elena Fortún (Madrid, 1886 – Madrid, 1953) was the literary name of Encarnación Aragoneses. She became one of the most important Spanish writers of children's literature in the twentieth century and the creator of Celia. Her stories accompanied generations of children and gave space to a curious, imaginative voice full of questions. Celia was created by Elena Fortún during a time of great change in Spain.

The Spanish Civil War (1936–1939) transformed the lives of many people. Elena Fortún went into exile in Argentina, where she continued writing. After the war, Spain entered a new period. Under the Franco dictatorship, publications could be reviewed and subjected to censorship.

What is censorship?

It is the control of what can be published, circulated, or made available to readers.

Open the book. Read. Listen to Celia.

title: Bird Library Exhibition: Cube Game
description:
Visit the first floor of Bird LIbrary to check out Cube Game: The Rubik's Cube and Other Dimensional Puzzle Games. 

Hungarian Architect and professor of design Ernő Rubik invented the cube in 1974, following his interest in three-dimensional geometry and the relationship between dimensional shapes. Originally known as the Magic Cube, it was rebranded as the Rubik’s Cube upon its worldwide release in 1980, quickly becoming the trendy must-have novelty of the decade. By the early 1980s, millions were attempting to solve its not-so simple challenge: arranging six faces of colored squares so that each displayed a single color. The Cube’s breakout success generated an entire industry of related products. Variations on the original design appeared in numerous shapes, sizes, and configurations, while other mechanical puzzles, including Rubik’s Snake, offered unique ways to manipulate geometric forms. Competing manufacturers introduced their own puzzles, with unauthorized copies and imitations became commonplace. The Cube also inspired board games, card games, promotional merchandise, and an extensive assortment of instructional books promising to reveal the secrets of solving it for a meager sum. Its influence extended well beyond the toy industry. The Cube became a fixture of popular culture, appearing in television programs, films, advertisements, cartoons, and comics. Closely associated with the 1980s, it has become a visual symbol of the decade. For some, solving the Cube became an obsessive pastime. Speedcubing developed into a highly competitive international sport, with hopefuls refining techniques to solve the complex puzzles in shorter and shorter times. Advances in technology brought robotic systems into the competition, showing that a handheld toy may serve as a serious challenge in mathematics, engineering, and computer science. This exhibition explores the Rubik’s Cube as both a puzzle and cultural phenomenon, tracing its development, commercial success, numerous offshoots, and continuing influence. From early examples and instructional guides to unusual variations and contemporary speedcubing, the objects presented here illustrate how a deceptively simple invention became a lasting part of popular culture. Few toys are as culturally iconic yet intellectually frustrating as the Rubik’s Cube.

Curated by Stephen Singer and Abigail Traska.

Game On!: Titles from the Bird Library Board Game Collection featured in the Miron case.

What do the Sheriff of Nottingham, the pandemic and exploding kittens have in common? They're all subjects of board and card games from Bird Library's game collection, located in the first-floor Learning Commons. Whether you're looking to do a puzzle, topple a Jenga tower or take a Risk, we have them all, free to borrow!

title: Class of 2028 Senior Class Marshal Applications
description:
Calling all juniors! Apply to be the Class of 2028 Senior Class Marshals.

Senior Class Marshals are Syracuse University's most committed and thoughtful students. They are distinguished individuals who exemplify the spirit of the senior class, embody One University, exhibit academic excellence and have excelled during their time at Syracuse. Each year, two Syracuse University rising seniors will be selected to serve as the all-University student representatives for their graduating class. During their senior year, they will have unique opportunities to engage with various University stakeholders, help select their Commencement speaker and discuss their student experience and offer constructive suggestions with senior administrators.

The deadline to apply is Friday, Jan. 15, 2027, 11:59 p.m.

Referrals

If you would like to refer a student for Senior Class Marshal and understand the requirements and expectations, please submit the reference form.

title: Family Support Navigator Applications
description:
Family Support Navigators (FSNs) serve as a vital resource and support system for parents, families and supporters of students enrolled at Syracuse University. This is a paid position for undergraduate students at Syracuse University, providing support during Summer Family/Supporter Orientation.

Students interested in becoming a Family Support Navigator must meet the following qualifications.

  • Be a full-time Syracuse University undergraduate student.
  • Maintain a cumulative GPA of at least 2.5.
  • Must give permission to verify good standing through Community Standards.
  • Must be on campus for the Spring 2027 semester.
  • Must be able to attend necessary trainings and events.
  • Have no work or co-curricular conflicts during any of the orientation session dates.

Family Support Navigator applications are due Sunday, Nov. 22. Interested students should apply online.

title: Helen Zughaib: Patterns of Migration
description:
August 25 - May 8, 2027

For the sixth iteration of The Art Wall Project, Helen Zughaib ’81 uses her characteristic bright color palette and intricate patterns to explore the stories of people’s displacement from their homes. By painting migration narratives from her own family’s history and our contemporary experiences, Zughaib considers how this global movement of individuals has shaped America as we know it today.

title: Mark and Pearle Clements Internship Award Applications
description:
The Mark and Pearle Clements Internship Awards are intended to enable Syracuse University students to undertake unique summer internships that they have developed on their own initiative and that would not be possible to undertake without financial help. The objective is that students create their own internship, working under the guidance and supervision of an experienced professional who can help them explore opportunities that link theory with practice in their fields of career interest.

Eligibility

  • Syracuse University juniors and master’s degree students of all majors are eligible to apply.
  • Academic credit may be earned for participation in these internships, but is not required.

Please contact Student Employment and Internship Support at cuseworks@syr.edu with questions or for more information.

title: Reclaimed: The Art of Recology
description:
September 1 - December 11, 2026

Reclaimed: The Art of Recology presents a survey of 33 artists who were selected to participate in Recology’s Artist-in-Residence program, which began in 1990. Armed with safety gear and a shopping cart, each of these artists have scavenging privileges in the Public Reuse and Recycling Area—what most artists refer to as “The Big Store”—to recycle and reclaim the discarded waste as imagined art objects. Through introspective, playful, and highly original explorations, the artists reveal the hidden stories our rubbish tells us about our complex relationship with the world, while highlighting the need to create sustainable communities.

This exhibition is curated by Emilee Enders. The exhibition tour is organized by Bedford Gallery at the Lesher Center for the Arts, Walnut Creek, CA.

title: Space and the Sacred: Letterio Calapai's Prints
description:
August 25 - December 11, 2026

Between the 1940s and his death in 1993, the printmaker Letterio Calapai produced dozens of works about outer space and Catholic subjects. This exhibition examines how his art transformed as these subjects evolved during his lifetime and reveals how one man understood the changing world around him.

This exhibition was curated by Julia Neufeld G’23 G’24. We gratefully acknowledge the Dryer Family Foundation for supporting this project.

title: The Promise of Public Service Exhibit
description:
The Maxwell School will be the inaugural host of the traveling exhibit “The Promise of Public Service” curated by the National Academy of Public Administration and showcasing public servants at all levels from across America, past and present.

The traveling exhibit is part of the Academy’s yearlong “Celebration of the American Public Servant,” dedicated to strengthening American democracy and public service as we honor the nation’s 250th anniversary.

The full exhibit was showcased at the Library of Congress during the Celebration of the American Public Servant 250 Gala in June, with the traveling exhibit on display in the Maxwell Hall foyer through the fall semester.

title: SCRC Exhibition "We Demand! A Legacy of Activism in America"
description:
Since the country’s founding, the American people have shaped—and continue to shape—a more just and equitable future for current and future generations. For decades, Syracuse University Libraries’ Special Collections Research Center (SCRC) has collected materials related to histories of activism and social reform in America that illustrate how advancements in rights were made possible by those who came before. This tireless pursuit and ongoing work of individuals and collective groups who have come together to push for change—not always seen during their lifetimes—in the face of extraordinary challenges and circumstances is documented within this exhibition.

Visitors can explore traces of resistance and perseverance in the form of publications, posters, protest signs, photographs, demands, newsletters, and more that document the critical role of activism in challenging injustice and securing greater freedoms for all.

The exhibition was curated by Courtney Hicks, SCRC Lead Curator and Curator of Plastics and Historical Artifacts, Jana Rosinski, SCRC Instruction and Education Librarian, and Lindy Smith, SCRC Assistant Director.

The exhibition was curated by Courtney Hicks, SCRC Lead Curator and Curator of Plastics and Historical Artifacts, Jana Rosinski, SCRC Instruction and Education Librarian, and Lindy Smith, SCRC Assistant Director.

title: Chemistry Colloquium: Qing Lin
description:
The Department of Chemistry in the College of Arts and Sciences is pleased to welcome Qing Lin, distinguished professor of chemistry at the University at Buffalo.

Title: Harnessing Chemical Reactivity for Biomedical Research

Abstract: There has been a growing interest recently in utilizing chemical reactivity directly to track biomolecular dynamics in living systems and design covalent ligands for biomedical applications. In this talk, I will describe our long-standing efforts in harnessing the highly reactive nitrile imine 1,3-dipoles by masking them in either the photoreactive tetrazole form or the stable hydrazonyl sultone tautomers for bioorthogonal ligation reactions in living systems. In conjunction with a genetically encoded strained alkene amino acid, spiro[2.3]hex-1-ene-lysine (SphK), and an alkyne amino acid, bicyclo[6.1.0]non-4-yn-9-ylmethanol-lysine (BCNK), these bioorthogonal reagents permit site-specific fluorescent labeling of GCGR and GLP-1R ¾ two members of the class B G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) family implicated in diabetes and obesity ¾ in live cells. In addition, I will discuss our recent efforts in harnessing the proximity-driven crosslinking reactivity of a genetically encoded electrophilic amino acids, beta-lactam-lysine (BeLaK), to generate the rigidified, bioactive, cell-penetrating monobodies as well as the covalent nanobody-based ligands to target tumor-associated antigens such as EGFR for therapeutic applications.

title: Finding Your Voice: From Ideas to Lyrics Workshop Series with Erika Turner
description:
Get ready to turn your ideas into lyrics with Erika Turner in this fun, two-part workshop series. Have you ever wanted to write a song but didn't know where to start? Does writer's block halt your creativity? If so, join this fun, creative, hands-on songwriting workshop where you'll turn your thoughts, experiences, and emotions into lyrics. Learn the basics of songwriting, explore creative writing techniques, develop a memorable hook or chorus, and discover your unique voice as a songwriter. No prior songwriting experience is necessary. Just bring your ideas, creativity, and confidence.

About The Artist

Erika Lovette (Turner) is a soulful singer, songwriter, and creative artist from Syracuse, New York, whose music blends the richness of R&B, Hip Hop, and Jazz with heartfelt storytelling and raw emotion. Singing and writing since the age of 16, Erika has developed a sound that is both authentic and expressive, drawing inspiration from the legendary artists who have shaped contemporary soul music while creating a voice and style uniquely her own. Erika uses her artistry to explore love, life, resilience, relationships, self-discovery, and the experiences that shape us. Her music invites listeners into moments that are deeply personal yet universally relatable. Whether delivering a soulful ballad or an upbeat, empowering groove, Erika brings warmth, honesty, and emotion to every performance. Her catalog includes original releases such as, Love Life and Everything in Between, “We Found Love,” a collaboration with her brother Darvin Lovette, and “Do Not Disturb.” Her empowering song “Unbreakable” reflects her commitment to using music as a source of strength, encouragement, and self-love, particularly for women navigating life's challenges. Erika's artistry extends beyond music. She is also an entrepreneur and the owner of Love Line Jewelry & Designs, where she channels her creativity into handcrafted jewelry and unique fiber-art creations. Her life as an educator, artist, and entrepreneur reflects a common thread: a desire to create, inspire, connect, and encourage others to embrace who they are. As Erika continues to grow her musical journey, she remains committed to creating music that feels good, tells a story, and leaves a lasting impression. Music isn't simply something she does—it is another way she expresses her heart, celebrates her journey, and connects with the world around her.

title: ‘Cuse Coats for Community
description:
This November, Syracuse University is inviting faculty, staff and students to help keep Central New York neighbors warm this winter through ‘Cuse Coats for Community. From Monday, Nov. 16 through Friday, Nov. 20 the campus community can drop off new or gently used coats at collection bins across campus. All donated coats will go directly to InterFaith Works to be distributed to community members in need. Children’s coats are needed most, though InterFaith Works is happy to accept coats of all sizes.

Collection bins will be available at the following locations: 

  • Hendricks Chapel near People’s Place Café
  • Bird Library on the first floor by the stairs facing Waverly Avenue
  • The Nancy Cantor Warehouse on the first floor by the DPS office
  • 610 Skytop Road in the Human Resources lobby area
  • The National Veterans Resource Center on the bottom floor by the Gallery
  • Sims Hall in the Department of Public Safety lobby
  • Crouse-Hinds Hall on the first floor behind the front desk

Those who don’t have a coat to give or who would like to support the drive in another way can contribute through an Amazon Wishlist set up by InterFaith Works. Items ordered from the list are delivered directly to InterFaith Works.

title: Biblio Gallery Exhibit: Celia: A Story that Persists
description:
The new Biblio Gallery exhibit on the 4th floor of Bird Library was curated by Juliana Acosta Gil G'27 (College of Arts and Sciences). 

Elena Fortún (Madrid, 1886 – Madrid, 1953) seudónimo de Encarnación Aragoneses Urquijo y la creadora de la zaga Celia. Sus historias acompañaron a niñas y niños y dieron espacio a una voz infantil curiosa, imaginativa y llena de preguntas. Celia nació en las páginas de Elena Fortún durante un momento de grandes cambios en España.

La Guerra Civil (1936–1939) transformó la vida de muchas personas. Elena Fortún se exilió en Argentina, donde continuó escribiendo. Después de la guerra, comenzó una nueva etapa en España. Bajo la dictadura franquista, las publicaciones podían ser revisadas y sometidas a censura.

¿Qué es la censura?

Es el control sobre lo que puede publicarse, circular o llegar a los lectores.

Abre el libro. Lee. Escucha a Celia.

Elena Fortún (Madrid, 1886 – Madrid, 1953) was the literary name of Encarnación Aragoneses. She became one of the most important Spanish writers of children's literature in the twentieth century and the creator of Celia. Her stories accompanied generations of children and gave space to a curious, imaginative voice full of questions. Celia was created by Elena Fortún during a time of great change in Spain.

The Spanish Civil War (1936–1939) transformed the lives of many people. Elena Fortún went into exile in Argentina, where she continued writing. After the war, Spain entered a new period. Under the Franco dictatorship, publications could be reviewed and subjected to censorship.

What is censorship?

It is the control of what can be published, circulated, or made available to readers.

Open the book. Read. Listen to Celia.

title: Bird Library Exhibition: Cube Game
description:
Visit the first floor of Bird LIbrary to check out Cube Game: The Rubik's Cube and Other Dimensional Puzzle Games. 

Hungarian Architect and professor of design Ernő Rubik invented the cube in 1974, following his interest in three-dimensional geometry and the relationship between dimensional shapes. Originally known as the Magic Cube, it was rebranded as the Rubik’s Cube upon its worldwide release in 1980, quickly becoming the trendy must-have novelty of the decade. By the early 1980s, millions were attempting to solve its not-so simple challenge: arranging six faces of colored squares so that each displayed a single color. The Cube’s breakout success generated an entire industry of related products. Variations on the original design appeared in numerous shapes, sizes, and configurations, while other mechanical puzzles, including Rubik’s Snake, offered unique ways to manipulate geometric forms. Competing manufacturers introduced their own puzzles, with unauthorized copies and imitations became commonplace. The Cube also inspired board games, card games, promotional merchandise, and an extensive assortment of instructional books promising to reveal the secrets of solving it for a meager sum. Its influence extended well beyond the toy industry. The Cube became a fixture of popular culture, appearing in television programs, films, advertisements, cartoons, and comics. Closely associated with the 1980s, it has become a visual symbol of the decade. For some, solving the Cube became an obsessive pastime. Speedcubing developed into a highly competitive international sport, with hopefuls refining techniques to solve the complex puzzles in shorter and shorter times. Advances in technology brought robotic systems into the competition, showing that a handheld toy may serve as a serious challenge in mathematics, engineering, and computer science. This exhibition explores the Rubik’s Cube as both a puzzle and cultural phenomenon, tracing its development, commercial success, numerous offshoots, and continuing influence. From early examples and instructional guides to unusual variations and contemporary speedcubing, the objects presented here illustrate how a deceptively simple invention became a lasting part of popular culture. Few toys are as culturally iconic yet intellectually frustrating as the Rubik’s Cube.

Curated by Stephen Singer and Abigail Traska.

Game On!: Titles from the Bird Library Board Game Collection featured in the Miron case.

What do the Sheriff of Nottingham, the pandemic and exploding kittens have in common? They're all subjects of board and card games from Bird Library's game collection, located in the first-floor Learning Commons. Whether you're looking to do a puzzle, topple a Jenga tower or take a Risk, we have them all, free to borrow!

title: Reclaimed: The Art of Recology
description:
September 1 - December 11, 2026

Reclaimed: The Art of Recology presents a survey of 33 artists who were selected to participate in Recology’s Artist-in-Residence program, which began in 1990. Armed with safety gear and a shopping cart, each of these artists have scavenging privileges in the Public Reuse and Recycling Area—what most artists refer to as “The Big Store”—to recycle and reclaim the discarded waste as imagined art objects. Through introspective, playful, and highly original explorations, the artists reveal the hidden stories our rubbish tells us about our complex relationship with the world, while highlighting the need to create sustainable communities.

This exhibition is curated by Emilee Enders. The exhibition tour is organized by Bedford Gallery at the Lesher Center for the Arts, Walnut Creek, CA.

title: Space and the Sacred: Letterio Calapai's Prints
description:
August 25 - December 11, 2026

Between the 1940s and his death in 1993, the printmaker Letterio Calapai produced dozens of works about outer space and Catholic subjects. This exhibition examines how his art transformed as these subjects evolved during his lifetime and reveals how one man understood the changing world around him.

This exhibition was curated by Julia Neufeld G’23 G’24. We gratefully acknowledge the Dryer Family Foundation for supporting this project.

title: The Promise of Public Service Exhibit
description:
The Maxwell School will be the inaugural host of the traveling exhibit “The Promise of Public Service” curated by the National Academy of Public Administration and showcasing public servants at all levels from across America, past and present.

The traveling exhibit is part of the Academy’s yearlong “Celebration of the American Public Servant,” dedicated to strengthening American democracy and public service as we honor the nation’s 250th anniversary.

The full exhibit was showcased at the Library of Congress during the Celebration of the American Public Servant 250 Gala in June, with the traveling exhibit on display in the Maxwell Hall foyer through the fall semester.

title: SCRC Exhibition "We Demand! A Legacy of Activism in America"
description:
Since the country’s founding, the American people have shaped—and continue to shape—a more just and equitable future for current and future generations. For decades, Syracuse University Libraries’ Special Collections Research Center (SCRC) has collected materials related to histories of activism and social reform in America that illustrate how advancements in rights were made possible by those who came before. This tireless pursuit and ongoing work of individuals and collective groups who have come together to push for change—not always seen during their lifetimes—in the face of extraordinary challenges and circumstances is documented within this exhibition.

Visitors can explore traces of resistance and perseverance in the form of publications, posters, protest signs, photographs, demands, newsletters, and more that document the critical role of activism in challenging injustice and securing greater freedoms for all.

The exhibition was curated by Courtney Hicks, SCRC Lead Curator and Curator of Plastics and Historical Artifacts, Jana Rosinski, SCRC Instruction and Education Librarian, and Lindy Smith, SCRC Assistant Director.

title: Teaching Assistant Coffee Hour
description:
The TA Coffee Hour, a great place to talk teaching, troubleshoot challenges, and connect across campus, is back!

This informal session, held twice per week on a biweekly schedule, is a chance to take a break, grab a snack, and talk about all things Teaching Assistant with other TAs and Teaching Mentors (TMs).

Each session kicks off with a starting theme, like building classroom community or navigating conflict, but where the conversation goes is up to you. Whether you're facing tough classroom dynamics, looking for feedback, or just want to hear how others are handling similar challenges, this is your space.

Come to share, listen, swap strategies, and workshop real situations in a relaxed, supportive setting. TAs from all departments and at all levels of experience are welcome.

Light refreshments provided. Curiosity and questions are encouraged.

title: Ethical GeoAI: Data, Algorithms and Critical Futures
description:
GeoAI is rapidly reshaping how researchers and practitioners understand cities, communities and socio-spatial inequalities. Along with new analytical opportunities, GeoAI also raises concerns around bias, privacy, fairness and environmental costs.

This talk highlights emerging debates about GeoAI and ethics and offers a framework for integrating GeoAI in ways that are both innovative and socially responsible. This lecture by Yue Lin is part of Geography Awareness Week, sponsored by the Geography and the Environment Department and the Community Geography program.

Yue Lin is an assistant professor in the Department of Geography and Geographic Information Science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

title: Reading Psalms Together
description:
Reading Psalms Together is a weekly Bible study that invites students, faculty, and staff to slow down, reflect, and encounter God through the rich prayers and poetry of the Psalms. Whether you are discerning your vocation, seeking comfort during a difficult season, asking life's deeper questions, or simply longing for a space of spiritual renewal, this gathering offers a welcoming community where you can explore Scripture alongside others. No prior Bible knowledge is required—only a willingness to come as you are and journey together. 

For more information, please check Hendricks Chapel’s Christian Protestant Chaplaincy — United Methodist web page.

title: Innovating the Orange Experience: How SU is Using Technology & AI to Shape the Future
description:
About the Event

Syracuse University is embracing digital transformation and artificial intelligence to enhance the student experience, advance research, and improve campus operations. Recently, Syracuse became one of the first universities in the United States to provide campuswide access to Claude for Education, Anthropic’s AI platform designed for academic settings.

Join Jeffrey Rubin, Syracuse University’s Chief Digital Officer and Interim Dean of the School of Information Studies, to learn how the University is integrating AI and technology into higher education and how the iSchool is preparing students to lead in an increasingly technology-driven world.

Meet the Speaker 

Jeffrey Rubin
Senior Vice President and Chief Digital Officer
Interim Dean, School of Information Studies
Professor of Practice, School of Information Studies

Jeffrey Rubin is Syracuse University’s inaugural Senior Vice President for Digital Transformation and Chief Digital Officer, Interim Dean of the iSchool, and a Professor of Practice. He oversees Information Technology Services and leads the University’s digital transformation efforts, focusing on digital innovation, data strategy, and the integration of artificial intelligence in higher education.

Rubin began his Syracuse University journey as an undergraduate in 1991 and has been a member of the iSchool faculty since 1996. He teaches more than 500 students annually and founded SIDEARM Sports, a digital fan engagement platform for college athletics. Following its acquisition by Learfield in 2014, he served as Executive Vice President of Digital, leading more than 200 employees and expanding the platform to serve over 95% of NCAA Division I institutions.

Today, Rubin helps shape Syracuse University’s digital strategy, connecting technology, data, and AI with the needs of students, faculty, staff, and the broader Orange community.

title: Tough Topic Tuesday: Public Enemy #1 - When Does Accountability Go Too Far?
description:
When does accountability become harassment, retaliation or another form of harm? In an age of social media and public call-outs, harmful behavior can quickly become a public conversation. This workshop explores what accountability looks like in the real world, on college campuses and in popular media, while examining what makes a consequence accountable rather than retaliatory.

Participants will explore different approaches to responding to bias and harmful behavior, while also considering the impact of more harmful tactics such as doxxing, threats and online harassment. Through guided dialogue and interactive scenarios, participants will examine what makes accountability effective and proportional, and how identity, power and social status can influence who receives accountability and how it is experienced.

title: ‘Cuse Coats for Community
description:
This November, Syracuse University is inviting faculty, staff and students to help keep Central New York neighbors warm this winter through ‘Cuse Coats for Community. Collection bins will be available at the following locations:

  • The Nancy Cantor Warehouse on the first floor by the DPS office
  • 610 Skytop Road in the Human Resources lobby area

  • Sims Hall in the Department of Public Safety lobby

Those who don’t have a coat to give or who would like to support the drive in another way can contribute through an Amazon Wishlist set up by InterFaith Works. Items ordered from the list are delivered directly to InterFaith Works.

title: Biblio Gallery Exhibit: Celia: A Story that Persists
description:
The new Biblio Gallery exhibit on the 4th floor of Bird Library was curated by Juliana Acosta Gil G'27 (College of Arts and Sciences). 

Elena Fortún (Madrid, 1886 – Madrid, 1953) seudónimo de Encarnación Aragoneses Urquijo y la creadora de la zaga Celia. Sus historias acompañaron a niñas y niños y dieron espacio a una voz infantil curiosa, imaginativa y llena de preguntas. Celia nació en las páginas de Elena Fortún durante un momento de grandes cambios en España.

La Guerra Civil (1936–1939) transformó la vida de muchas personas. Elena Fortún se exilió en Argentina, donde continuó escribiendo. Después de la guerra, comenzó una nueva etapa en España. Bajo la dictadura franquista, las publicaciones podían ser revisadas y sometidas a censura.

¿Qué es la censura?

Es el control sobre lo que puede publicarse, circular o llegar a los lectores.

Abre el libro. Lee. Escucha a Celia.

Elena Fortún (Madrid, 1886 – Madrid, 1953) was the literary name of Encarnación Aragoneses. She became one of the most important Spanish writers of children's literature in the twentieth century and the creator of Celia. Her stories accompanied generations of children and gave space to a curious, imaginative voice full of questions. Celia was created by Elena Fortún during a time of great change in Spain.

The Spanish Civil War (1936–1939) transformed the lives of many people. Elena Fortún went into exile in Argentina, where she continued writing. After the war, Spain entered a new period. Under the Franco dictatorship, publications could be reviewed and subjected to censorship.

What is censorship?

It is the control of what can be published, circulated, or made available to readers.

Open the book. Read. Listen to Celia.

title: Bird Library Exhibition: Cube Game
description:
Visit the first floor of Bird LIbrary to check out Cube Game: The Rubik's Cube and Other Dimensional Puzzle Games. 

Hungarian Architect and professor of design Ernő Rubik invented the cube in 1974, following his interest in three-dimensional geometry and the relationship between dimensional shapes. Originally known as the Magic Cube, it was rebranded as the Rubik’s Cube upon its worldwide release in 1980, quickly becoming the trendy must-have novelty of the decade. By the early 1980s, millions were attempting to solve its not-so simple challenge: arranging six faces of colored squares so that each displayed a single color. The Cube’s breakout success generated an entire industry of related products. Variations on the original design appeared in numerous shapes, sizes, and configurations, while other mechanical puzzles, including Rubik’s Snake, offered unique ways to manipulate geometric forms. Competing manufacturers introduced their own puzzles, with unauthorized copies and imitations became commonplace. The Cube also inspired board games, card games, promotional merchandise, and an extensive assortment of instructional books promising to reveal the secrets of solving it for a meager sum. Its influence extended well beyond the toy industry. The Cube became a fixture of popular culture, appearing in television programs, films, advertisements, cartoons, and comics. Closely associated with the 1980s, it has become a visual symbol of the decade. For some, solving the Cube became an obsessive pastime. Speedcubing developed into a highly competitive international sport, with hopefuls refining techniques to solve the complex puzzles in shorter and shorter times. Advances in technology brought robotic systems into the competition, showing that a handheld toy may serve as a serious challenge in mathematics, engineering, and computer science. This exhibition explores the Rubik’s Cube as both a puzzle and cultural phenomenon, tracing its development, commercial success, numerous offshoots, and continuing influence. From early examples and instructional guides to unusual variations and contemporary speedcubing, the objects presented here illustrate how a deceptively simple invention became a lasting part of popular culture. Few toys are as culturally iconic yet intellectually frustrating as the Rubik’s Cube.

Curated by Stephen Singer and Abigail Traska.

Game On!: Titles from the Bird Library Board Game Collection featured in the Miron case.

What do the Sheriff of Nottingham, the pandemic and exploding kittens have in common? They're all subjects of board and card games from Bird Library's game collection, located in the first-floor Learning Commons. Whether you're looking to do a puzzle, topple a Jenga tower or take a Risk, we have them all, free to borrow!

title: Class of 2028 Senior Class Marshal Applications
description:
Calling all juniors! Apply to be the Class of 2028 Senior Class Marshals.

Senior Class Marshals are Syracuse University's most committed and thoughtful students. They are distinguished individuals who exemplify the spirit of the senior class, embody One University, exhibit academic excellence and have excelled during their time at Syracuse. description:

By painting migration narratives from her own family’s history and our contemporary experiences, Zughaib considers how this global movement of individuals has shaped America as we know it today.

title: Reclaimed: The Art of Recology
description:
September 1 - December 11, 2026

Reclaimed: The Art of Recology presents a survey of 33 artists who were selected to participate in Recology’s Artist-in-Residence program, which began in 1990. Armed with safety gear and a shopping cart, each of these artists have scavenging privileges in the Public Reuse and Recycling Area—what most artists refer to as “The Big Store”—to recycle and reclaim the discarded waste as imagined art objects. Through introspective, playful, and highly original explorations, the artists reveal the hidden stories our rubbish tells us about our complex relationship with the world, while highlighting the need to create sustainable communities.

This exhibition is curated by Emilee Enders. The exhibition tour is organized by Bedford Gallery at the Lesher Center for the Arts, Walnut Creek, CA.

title: Space and the Sacred: Letterio Calapai's Prints
description:
August 25 - December 11, 2026

Between the 1940s and his death in 1993, the printmaker Letterio Calapai produced dozens of works about outer space and Catholic subjects. This exhibition examines how his art transformed as these subjects evolved during his lifetime and reveals how one man understood the changing world around him.

This exhibition was curated by Julia Neufeld G’23 G’24. We gratefully acknowledge the Dryer Family Foundation for supporting this project.

title: The Promise of Public Service Exhibit
description:
The Maxwell School will be the inaugural host of the traveling exhibit “The Promise of Public Service” curated by the National Academy of Public Administration and showcasing public servants at all levels from across America, past and present.

The traveling exhibit is part of the Academy’s yearlong “Celebration of the American Public Servant,” dedicated to strengthening American democracy and public service as we honor the nation’s 250th anniversary.

The full exhibit was showcased at the Library of Congress during the Celebration of the American Public Servant 250 Gala in June, with the traveling exhibit on display in the Maxwell Hall foyer through the fall semester.

title: SCRC Exhibition "We Demand! A Legacy of Activism in America"
description:
Since the country’s founding, the American people have shaped—and continue to shape—a more just and equitable future for current and future generations. For decades, Syracuse University Libraries’ Special Collections Research Center (SCRC) has collected materials related to histories of activism and social reform in America that illustrate how advancements in rights were made possible by those who came before. This tireless pursuit and ongoing work of individuals and collective groups who have come together to push for change—not always seen during their lifetimes—in the face of extraordinary challenges and circumstances is documented within this exhibition.

Visitors can explore traces of resistance and perseverance in the form of publications, posters, protest signs, photographs, demands, newsletters, and more that document the critical role of activism in challenging injustice and securing greater freedoms for all.

The exhibition was curated by Courtney Hicks, SCRC Lead Curator and Curator of Plastics and Historical Artifacts, Jana Rosinski, SCRC Instruction and Education Librarian, and Lindy Smith, SCRC Assistant Director.

This tireless pursuit and ongoing work of individuals and collective groups who have come together to push for change—not always seen during their lifetimes—in the face of extraordinary challenges and circumstances is documented within this exhibition. 

Visitors can explore traces of resistance and perseverance in the form of publications, posters, protest signs, photographs, demands, newsletters, and more that document the critical role of activism in challenging injustice and securing greater freedoms for all. 

The exhibition was curated by Courtney Hicks, SCRC Lead Curator and Curator of Plastics and Historical Artifacts, Jana Rosinski, SCRC Instruction and Education Librarian, and Lindy Smith, SCRC Assistant Director.

title: GIS (Geographic Information System) Day
description:
GIS stands for geographic information system, a type of technology used for mapping and data analysis. GIS Day is an opportunity to learn more about this technology and how it can transform research. To celebrate, the Geography and the Environment Department ise offering three events. Join for one, two or all three of them. 

Coffee and Creative Cartographies, 9:30-11:30 a.m.

Join us for coffee and create a map collage, disco maps, story maps (bring a laptop), and map icons with geography faculty and students researching at intersections of maps, art and storytelling. Come with any mapping questions and go as you please!

AI and Geospatial Technologies, 12–1:30 p.m.  

A round table discussion with Yue Lin (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) and invited guests on AI and geospatial technologies (GeoAI) and how they are being used (or not) in research, teaching and professional practice. Bring lunch and your questions. We'll have beverages and desserts!

GIS and Mapping Jobs Panel, 2–3:30 p.m. 

A panel discussion on career pathways in GIS and mapping. Snacks provided.

title: Better Together: Understanding Your Places of Influence
description:
The Office of People and Culture invites faculty and staff to join us for Core Workshop: Better Together: Understanding Your Places of Influence.

 

Phrases like, “There is strength in numbers,” or “Two are better than one,” highlight the value of working together. Yet influence, within a group, goes beyond merely being present; it is important to consider how influence is shared and what happens when some individuals or communities are excluded from contributing to it. In this workshop, we will reflect on the concept of influence: who has it, how it functions within groups, and why environments tend to be more sustainable when built collaboratively. 

 

AI Captioning will be provided.

 

Please register by November 17: Registration for Core Workshop – Better Together. A Zoom link will be sent to participants upon registration. 

 

For questions or concerns, contact Christina Papaleo at cpapaleo@syr.edu.

title: Wednesday Catholic Mass
description:
The SU / SUNY ESF Catholic Campus ministry at the SU Catholic Center offers a rich, vibrant ministry. Our mission is to build a strong community that is completely accepting, inclusive, and bound together, regardless of race, ethnicity, or sexual orientation, by God’s universal love. We demonstrate that love through the celebration of the sacraments, small faith-sharing groups, fellowship, volunteer service, music, and social action. 

We seek with all that we do to provide a welcoming, fun, and loving place for people to express their faith, to know that they are not alone and to discover the love that Jesus has for them. 

Our events, which occur at the Catholic Center (110 Walnut Place, across from the Whitman School of Management) unless otherwise indicated, are open to all. 

Also, the Catholic Center has study spaces (library and Great Room) and prayer spaces that could serve as an oasis for quiet meditation, focusing on mindfulness and centering on the Lord. 

For more information, please check Hendricks Chapel’s Roman Catholic Chaplaincy web page.

title: Explore Teacher Education at Syracuse University: Information Session
description:
Ready to take the next step toward becoming a teacher?

Join the Syracuse University School of Education for an upcoming information session to explore our graduate teacher education programs and find the pathway that’s right for you.

Whether you’re pursuing initial certification and do not yet hold a teaching certificate, or you already have certification and are looking to advance through a professional certification program, our teacher education programs can help you build the knowledge, skills, and experience to make an impact in today’s classrooms.

Register for this info session

During this session, you’ll learn more about:

  • Our graduate teacher education and certification programs
  • Initial certification pathways for students who do not currently hold a teaching certificate
  • Professional certification pathways for currently certified educators
  • Program structure, curriculum, and field experiences
  • Admissions requirements and application deadlines
  • New York State teacher certification requirements
  • What it’s like to study and prepare for a career in education at Syracuse University

You’ll also have the opportunity to ask questions and connect with School of Education staff & faculty about finding the program and certification pathway that best fits your goals.

Please note: This information session is primarily geared toward domestic students, as our teacher education programs lead to New York State teacher certification.

Witness to Injustice is a unique 2.5-hour interactive group teaching tool that uses participatory education to share the disturbing history of what Indigenous Peoples have experienced through colonization. The program seeks to foster truth, understanding and respect between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples in the part of the world now known as the United States, especially in the territory stewarded by people of the Onondaga Nation and other Haudenosaunee peoples.

This program was created in collaboration with KAIROS Canada. All are welcome.

title: Public Tour of "We Demand: A Legacy of Activism in America"
description:
Syracuse University Libraries' Special Collections Research Center (SCRC) is offering public tours of the current exhibition, We Demand: A Legacy of Activism in America. The tours will be led by two of the curators of the exhibition, Jana Rosinski, SCRC Instruction and Education Librarian, and Lindy Smith, SCRC Assistant Director.

Since this country’s founding, the American people have shaped—and continue to shape—a more just and equitable future. For decades, Syracuse University Libraries’ Special Collections Research Center (SCRC) has collected materials related to histories of activism and social reform in America that illustrate how advancements in rights were made possible by those who came before. This tireless pursuit and ongoing work of individuals and collective groups who have come together to push for change—not always seen during their lifetimes—in the face of extraordinary challenges and circumstances are documented within this exhibition. Traces of resistance and perseverance in the form of posters, protest signs, photographs, demands, newsletters, and more represent the critical role of activism in challenging injustice and securing greater freedoms in the United States. We invite you to consider which legacies of activism have shaped your own experiences, what movements and causes resonate with you, and which stories remain to be told.

Tours are free and open to the public. Spots are limited, so registration is required. REGISTER HERE

The exhibition will be on view at the Special Collections Research Center, Bird Library, 6th floor gallery through the end of December 2026.

If you require an accommodation, please email Max Wagh, mlwagh@syr.edu.

title: Salaam Shalom: Learning Hebrew and Arabic as an Interfaith Practice
description:
Salaam Shalom: Learning Hebrew and Arabic as an Interfaith Practice

title: Henry V
description:
By William Shakespeare | Directed by John Tufts

Nov. 13 – 21 | Opening Night: Nov. 14

Pressed by powerful nobles and church leaders to reclaim England’s sovereignty over France, the young, rebellious King Henry V of England raises an army and carves his way to Agincourt, where his troops, depleted and exhausted, must face the enemy head-on. But with dissension in the ranks, Henry will have to prove himself a strong and legitimate ruler if he’s to inspire his men to lay down their lives for their country and their king. Shakespeare’s thrilling history play ponders the true cost of winning in the epic game of thrones.

title: ‘Cuse Coats for Community
description:
This November, Syracuse University is inviting faculty, staff and students to help keep Central New York neighbors warm this winter through ‘Cuse Coats for Community. From Monday, Nov. 16 through Friday, Nov. 20 the campus community can drop off new or gently used coats at collection bins across campus. All donated coats will go directly to InterFaith Works to be distributed to community members in need. Children’s coats are needed most, though InterFaith Works is happy to accept coats of all sizes.

Collection bins will be available at the following locations: 

  • Hendricks Chapel near People’s Place Café
  • Bird Library on the first floor by the stairs facing Waverly Avenue
  • The Nancy Cantor Warehouse on the first floor by the DPS office
  • 610 Skytop Road in the Human Resources lobby area
  • The National Veterans Resource Center on the bottom floor by the Gallery
  • Sims Hall in the Department of Public Safety lobby
  • Crouse-Hinds Hall on the first floor behind the front desk

Those who don’t have a coat to give or who would like to support the drive in another way can contribute through an Amazon Wishlist set up by InterFaith Works. Items ordered from the list are delivered directly to InterFaith Works.

title: Biblio Gallery Exhibit: Celia: A Story that Persists
description:
The new Biblio Gallery exhibit on the 4th floor of Bird Library was curated by Juliana Acosta Gil G'27 (College of Arts and Sciences). 

Elena Fortún (Madrid, 1886 – Madrid, 1953) seudónimo de Encarnación Aragoneses Urquijo y la creadora de la zaga Celia. Sus historias acompañaron a niñas y niños y dieron espacio a una voz infantil curiosa, imaginativa y llena de preguntas. Celia nació en las páginas de Elena Fortún durante un momento de grandes cambios en España.

La Guerra Civil (1936–1939) transformó la vida de muchas personas. Elena Fortún se exilió en Argentina, donde continuó escribiendo. Después de la guerra, comenzó una nueva etapa en España. Bajo la dictadura franquista, las publicaciones podían ser revisadas y sometidas a censura.

¿Qué es la censura?

Es el control sobre lo que puede publicarse, circular o llegar a los lectores.

Abre el libro. Lee. Escucha a Celia.

Elena Fortún (Madrid, 1886 – Madrid, 1953) was the literary name of Encarnación Aragoneses. She became one of the most important Spanish writers of children's literature in the twentieth century and the creator of Celia. Her stories accompanied generations of children and gave space to a curious, imaginative voice full of questions. Celia was created by Elena Fortún during a time of great change in Spain.

The Spanish Civil War (1936–1939) transformed the lives of many people. Elena Fortún went into exile in Argentina, where she continued writing. After the war, Spain entered a new period. Under the Franco dictatorship, publications could be reviewed and subjected to censorship.

What is censorship?

It is the control of what can be published, circulated, or made available to readers.

Open the book. Read. Listen to Celia.

title: Bird Library Exhibition: Cube Game
description:
Visit the first floor of Bird LIbrary to check out Cube Game: The Rubik's Cube and Other Dimensional Puzzle Games. 

Hungarian Architect and professor of design Ernő Rubik invented the cube in 1974, following his interest in three-dimensional geometry and the relationship between dimensional shapes. Originally known as the Magic Cube, it was rebranded as the Rubik’s Cube upon its worldwide release in 1980, quickly becoming the trendy must-have novelty of the decade. By the early 1980s, millions were attempting to solve its not-so simple challenge: arranging six faces of colored squares so that each displayed a single color. The Cube’s breakout success generated an entire industry of related products. Variations on the original design appeared in numerous shapes, sizes, and configurations, while other mechanical puzzles, including Rubik’s Snake, offered unique ways to manipulate geometric forms. Competing manufacturers introduced their own puzzles, with unauthorized copies and imitations became commonplace. The Cube also inspired board games, card games, promotional merchandise, and an extensive assortment of instructional books promising to reveal the secrets of solving it for a meager sum. Its influence extended well beyond the toy industry. The Cube became a fixture of popular culture, appearing in television programs, films, advertisements, cartoons, and comics. Closely associated with the 1980s, it has become a visual symbol of the decade. For some, solving the Cube became an obsessive pastime. Speedcubing developed into a highly competitive international sport, with hopefuls refining techniques to solve the complex puzzles in shorter and shorter times. Advances in technology brought robotic systems into the competition, showing that a handheld toy may serve as a serious challenge in mathematics, engineering, and computer science. This exhibition explores the Rubik’s Cube as both a puzzle and cultural phenomenon, tracing its development, commercial success, numerous offshoots, and continuing influence. From early examples and instructional guides to unusual variations and contemporary speedcubing, the objects presented here illustrate how a deceptively simple invention became a lasting part of popular culture. Few toys are as culturally iconic yet intellectually frustrating as the Rubik’s Cube.

Curated by Stephen Singer and Abigail Traska.

Game On!: Titles from the Bird Library Board Game Collection featured in the Miron case.

What do the Sheriff of Nottingham, the pandemic and exploding kittens have in common? They're all subjects of board and card games from Bird Library's game collection, located in the first-floor Learning Commons. Whether you're looking to do a puzzle, topple a Jenga tower or take a Risk, we have them all, free to borrow!

title: Class of 2028 Senior Class Marshal Applications
description:
Calling all juniors! Apply to be the Class of 2028 Senior Class Marshals.

Senior Class Marshals are Syracuse University's most committed and thoughtful students. They are distinguished individuals who exemplify the spirit of the senior class, embody One University, exhibit academic excellence and have excelled during their time at Syracuse. Each year, two Syracuse University rising seniors will be selected to serve as the all-University student representatives for their graduating class. During their senior year, they will have unique opportunities to engage with various University stakeholders, help select their Commencement speaker and discuss their student experience and offer constructive suggestions with senior administrators.

The deadline to apply is Friday, Jan. 15, 2027, 11:59 p.m.

Referrals

If you would like to refer a student for Senior Class Marshal and understand the requirements and expectations, please submit the reference form.

title: Family Support Navigator Applications
description:
Family Support Navigators (FSNs) serve as a vital resource and support system for parents, families and supporters of students enrolled at Syracuse University. This is a paid position for undergraduate students at Syracuse University, providing support during Summer Family/Supporter Orientation.

Students interested in becoming a Family Support Navigator must meet the following qualifications.

  • Maintain a cumulative GPA of at least 2.5.
  • Must give permission to verify good standing through Community Standards.
  • Must be on campus for the Spring 2027 semester.
  • Must be able to attend necessary trainings and events.
  • Have no work or co-curricular conflicts during any of the orientation session dates.

Family Support Navigator applications are due Sunday, Nov. 22. Interested students should apply online.

title: Helen Zughaib: Patterns of Migration
description:
August 25 - May 8, 2027

For the sixth iteration of The Art Wall Project, Helen Zughaib ’81 uses her characteristic bright color palette and intricate patterns to explore the stories of people’s displacement from their homes. By painting migration narratives from her own family’s history and our contemporary experiences, Zughaib considers how this global movement of individuals has shaped America as we know it today.

title: Reclaimed: The Art of Recology
description:
September 1 - December 11, 2026

Reclaimed: The Art of Recology presents a survey of 33 artists who were selected to participate in Recology’s Artist-in-Residence program, which began in 1990. Armed with safety gear and a shopping cart, each of these artists have scavenging privileges in the Public Reuse and Recycling Area—what most artists refer to as “The Big Store”—to recycle and reclaim the discarded waste as imagined art objects. Through introspective, playful, and highly original explorations, the artists reveal the hidden stories our rubbish tells us about our complex relationship with the world, while highlighting the need to create sustainable communities.

This exhibition is curated by Emilee Enders. The exhibition tour is organized by Bedford Gallery at the Lesher Center for the Arts, Walnut Creek, CA.

title: Space and the Sacred: Letterio Calapai's Prints
description:
August 25 - December 11, 2026

Between the 1940s and his death in 1993, the printmaker Letterio Calapai produced dozens of works about outer space and Catholic subjects. This exhibition examines how his art transformed as these subjects evolved during his lifetime and reveals how one man understood the changing world around him.

This exhibition was curated by Julia Neufeld G’23 G’24. We gratefully acknowledge the Dryer Family Foundation for supporting this project.

title: The Promise of Public Service Exhibit
description:
The Maxwell School will be the inaugural host of the traveling exhibit “The Promise of Public Service” curated by the National Academy of Public Administration and showcasing public servants at all levels from across America, past and present.

The traveling exhibit is part of the Academy’s yearlong “Celebration of the American Public Servant,” dedicated to strengthening American democracy and public service as we honor the nation’s 250th anniversary.

The full exhibit was showcased at the Library of Congress during the Celebration of the American Public Servant 250 Gala in June, with the traveling exhibit on display in the Maxwell Hall foyer through the fall semester.

title: SCRC Exhibition "We Demand! A Legacy of Activism in America"
description:
Since the country’s founding, the American people have shaped—and continue to shape—a more just and equitable future for current and future generations. For decades, Syracuse University Libraries’ Special Collections Research Center (SCRC) has collected materials related to histories of activism and social reform in America that illustrate how advancements in rights were made possible by those who came before. This tireless pursuit and ongoing work of individuals and collective groups who have come together to push for change—not always seen during their lifetimes—in the face of extraordinary challenges and circumstances is documented within this exhibition.

Visitors can explore traces of resistance and perseverance in the form of publications, posters, protest signs, photographs, demands, newsletters, and more that document the critical role of activism in challenging injustice and securing greater freedoms for all.

The exhibition was curated by Courtney Hicks, SCRC Lead Curator and Curator of Plastics and Historical Artifacts, Jana Rosinski, SCRC Instruction and Education Librarian, and Lindy Smith, SCRC Assistant Director.

title: Conversations in Conflict Studies: Deferred Water Injustice (DWI)
description:
Despite sitting within the world’s largest river delta, Dhaka, the capital of Bangladesh, has become increasingly dependent on groundwater as rapid urbanization and severe surface-water pollution have transformed the city’s waterscape. While policy seeks to reduce this dependence through more sustainable alternatives, Dhaka’s expanding peri-urban frontier, which is also an industrial belt, still relies almost entirely on privately extracted groundwater.

Drawing on archival research and fieldwork across peri-urban settlements, Avia Nahreen examines households’ dependence on pumps that draw from aquifers government agencies monitor sparsely. She terms the water injustices arising from this arrangement “deferred water injustice”: the production of present-day water abundance by displacing its ecological and social costs into the future, while selective measurement keeps those costs politically invisible.

Avia Nahreen is a Ph.D. candidate in the Geography and the Environment Department. Her research examines urban water politics, environmental injustice and the layered experiences of water infrastructure in Dhaka. She explores groundwater dependence, colonial water legacies and everyday struggles and possibilities surrounding water access.

Lunch will be provided.

title: Teaching Assistant Coffee Hour
description:
The TA Coffee Hour, a great place to talk teaching, troubleshoot challenges, and connect across campus, is back!

This informal session, held twice per week on a biweekly schedule, is a chance to take a break, grab a snack, and talk about all things Teaching Assistant with other TAs and Teaching Mentors (TMs).

Each session kicks off with a starting theme, like building classroom community or navigating conflict, but where the conversation goes is up to you. Whether you're facing tough classroom dynamics, looking for feedback, or just want to hear how others are handling similar challenges, this is your space.

Come to share, listen, swap strategies, and workshop real situations in a relaxed, supportive setting. TAs from all departments and at all levels of experience are welcome.

Light refreshments provided. Curiosity and questions are encouraged.

title: LAPPRI Research Seminar: Networks of Prescribed Interaction in Chilean Environmental Governance
description:
The Latin America Policy Process Research Initiative (LAPPRI) aims to advance established and emerging policy process theories in order to enhance scholarly understanding of policymaking in Latin America. The LAPPRI Research Seminar Series features scholars from around the world dedicated to researching policy process dynamics across the region.

Presenters:

Karina Arias Yurisch (Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile) and Karina Retamal Soto (Universidad de Chile)

Title:

Networks of Prescribed Interaction in Chilean Environmental Governance

Abstract:

Environmental policies increasingly depend on coordination among multiple public agencies, yet the coordination they prescribe is rarely examined at the moment of design. Decontamination plans are a clear case. A single plan addresses diverse problems, some with identifiable sources that authorities can target directly and others with diffuse sources whose resolution depends on many interdependent actors.

We ask whether this difference leaves an imprint on how policies prescribe coordination. We argue that the nature of the problem shapes policy design, because the instruments feasible for each problem carry rules that define who must interact with whom and therefore produce distinct architectures of prescribed coordination. We examine this argument in two Chilean decontamination plans that govern different environmental media, the Villarrica Lake Basin Water Pollution Control Plan and the Santiago Metropolitan Region Atmospheric Prevention and Decontamination Plan.

Using Institutional Grammar 2.0, we decompose each plan into institutional statements and reconstruct multilevel networks of prescribed interaction among public agencies, among tasks, and between agencies and the tasks the rules assign them. We then apply network motif analysis and multilevel Exponential Random Graph Models to compare the coordination prescribed for identifiable-source and diffuse problems.

In both plans, coordination is anchored in managing agencies, while shared responsibility, in which coordinated agencies converge on the same tasks, intensifies where sources are diffuse. Each plan thus rests on a common managerial backbone that adds distributed convergence in proportion to the interdependence of each problem. The comparison across water and air suggests that the nature of the problem, more than the policy domain, drives the coordination that formal rules create. It also offers a way to anticipate the coordination demands placed on subnational actors.

Join us for an informative session on applying to the National Institutes of Health (NIH) National Institute of General Medical Sciences (NIGMS) Maximizing Investigators' Research Award (MIRA) (R35) grant program. title: Physics Colloquium: "Teaching Students How to Learn in an AI World"
description:
Please join the Department of Physics in welcoming Aaron Titus, Teaching Professor in the Department of Physics at North Carolina State University, for his talk titled, "Teaching Students How to Learn in an AI World."

Aaron Titus is a Teaching Professor in the Department of Physics at North Carolina State University where he co-coordinates the two-semester sequence of calculus-based physics. In 1997, Aaron Titus and Larry Martin created WebAssign. Titus was a member of the Open Source Physics (OSP) team, led by Wolfgang Christian, that received the American Physical Society’s 2020 Excellence in Physics Education award. Titus is a collaborator on the development of VPython and Trinket and a co-author of the fifth edition of the textbook Matter and Interactions with Ruth Chabay, Bruce Sherwood and Steve Spicklemire. In 2026, Titus received the David Halliday and Robert Resnick Award for Excellence in Undergraduate Physics Teaching from AAPT.

Abstract: Here's a fairly common scenario: students consistently attend lecture, take detailed notes, attempt homework, get stuck on homework and use AI to get the answers. They think they "understand it" when they read the solution or watch lectures, and they are confident. Then, right before a test, they spend many hours reviewing notes and practicing solving problems, perhaps asking AI for additional problems to solve. When they fail the test, they are surprised because they "spent hours studying," and their methods mostly worked in high school. In order to reach this group of students, I now give a 1-hr, optional workshop on "how to learn" for students in our large, calculus-based physics course for engineers (1700+ students per semester). The key is metacognition -- thinking about your thinking. Across three semesters and more than 3,000 students in mechanics, students who attended the workshop had a 9-point higher gain from Test 1 to Test 2 than non-workshop students, and their higher gain persisted on later tests and the final exam. Furthermore, the workshop helped change students' initial perception of the course as a "weed out" course. While the context of my work is the introductory course, the principles are applicable to intermediate and advanced physics courses where students are also tempted to relegate "thinking tasks" to AI. Metacognition is the key to using AI effectively while avoiding cognitive surrender.

title: Yifan Luo | Visiting Artist Lecture Series
description:
Yifan Luo is a Baltimore-based illustrator, visual storyteller and educator.

Luo specializes in editorial narratives, comics and slices of life that explore current events, personal stories and sustainability. Her illustrations, reportage and comics have appeared in The Washington Post, The Baltimore Banner, Eater, The Nib and more.

Luo received a B.A. from Brown University and an M.F.A. in illustration practice from the Maryland Institute College of Art (MICA), where she has taught a graduate-level class on illustrated nonfiction and currently teaches a sketchbook intensive course. You can often find her collaborating with young writers at CHARM: Voices of Baltimore Youth.

The Visiting Artist Lecture Series, which features approximately 25 contemporary artists each semester, is free to attend and open to the public.

title: Henry V
description:
By William Shakespeare | Directed by John Tufts

Nov. 13 – 21 | Opening Night: Nov. 14

Pressed by powerful nobles and church leaders to reclaim England’s sovereignty over France, the young, rebellious King Henry V of England raises an army and carves his way to Agincourt, where his troops, depleted and exhausted, must face the enemy head-on. But with dissension in the ranks, Henry will have to prove himself a strong and legitimate ruler if he’s to inspire his men to lay down their lives for their country and their king. Shakespeare’s thrilling history play ponders the true cost of winning in the epic game of thrones.

title: ‘Cuse Coats for Community
description:
This November, Syracuse University is inviting faculty, staff and students to help keep Central New York neighbors warm this winter through ‘Cuse Coats for Community. From Monday, Nov. 16 through Friday, Nov. 20 the campus community can drop off new or gently used coats at collection bins across campus. All donated coats will go directly to InterFaith Works to be distributed to community members in need. Children’s coats are needed most, though InterFaith Works is happy to accept coats of all sizes.

Collection bins will be available at the following locations: 

  • Hendricks Chapel near People’s Place Café
  • Bird Library on the first floor by the stairs facing Waverly Avenue
  • The Nancy Cantor Warehouse on the first floor by the DPS office
  • 610 Skytop Road in the Human Resources lobby area
  • The National Veterans Resource Center on the bottom floor by the Gallery
  • Sims Hall in the Department of Public Safety lobby
  • Crouse-Hinds Hall on the first floor behind the front desk

Those who don’t have a coat to give or who would like to support the drive in another way can contribute through an Amazon Wishlist set up by InterFaith Works. Items ordered from the list are delivered directly to InterFaith Works.

title: Biblio Gallery Exhibit: Celia: A Story that Persists
description:
The new Biblio Gallery exhibit on the 4th floor of Bird Library was curated by Juliana Acosta Gil G'27 (College of Arts and Sciences). 

Elena Fortún (Madrid, 1886 – Madrid, 1953) seudónimo de Encarnación Aragoneses Urquijo y la creadora de la zaga Celia. Sus historias acompañaron a niñas y niños y dieron espacio a una voz infantil curiosa, imaginativa y llena de preguntas. Celia nació en las páginas de Elena Fortún durante un momento de grandes cambios en España.

La Guerra Civil (1936–1939) transformó la vida de muchas personas. Elena Fortún se exilió en Argentina, donde continuó escribiendo. Después de la guerra, comenzó una nueva etapa en España. Bajo la dictadura franquista, las publicaciones podían ser revisadas y sometidas a censura.

¿Qué es la censura?

Es el control sobre lo que puede publicarse, circular o llegar a los lectores.

Abre el libro. Lee. Escucha a Celia.

Elena Fortún (Madrid, 1886 – Madrid, 1953) was the literary name of Encarnación Aragoneses. She became one of the most important Spanish writers of children's literature in the twentieth century and the creator of Celia. Her stories accompanied generations of children and gave space to a curious, imaginative voice full of questions. Celia was created by Elena Fortún during a time of great change in Spain.

The Spanish Civil War (1936–1939) transformed the lives of many people. Elena Fortún went into exile in Argentina, where she continued writing. After the war, Spain entered a new period. Under the Franco dictatorship, publications could be reviewed and subjected to censorship.

What is censorship?

It is the control of what can be published, circulated, or made available to readers.

Open the book. Read. Listen to Celia.

title: Bird Library Exhibition: Cube Game
description:
Visit the first floor of Bird LIbrary to check out Cube Game: The Rubik's Cube and Other Dimensional Puzzle Games. 

Hungarian Architect and professor of design Ernő Rubik invented the cube in 1974, following his interest in three-dimensional geometry and the relationship between dimensional shapes. Originally known as the Magic Cube, it was rebranded as the Rubik’s Cube upon its worldwide release in 1980, quickly becoming the trendy must-have novelty of the decade. By the early 1980s, millions were attempting to solve its not-so simple challenge: arranging six faces of colored squares so that each displayed a single color. The Cube’s breakout success generated an entire industry of related products. Variations on the original design appeared in numerous shapes, sizes, and configurations, while other mechanical puzzles, including Rubik’s Snake, offered unique ways to manipulate geometric forms. Competing manufacturers introduced their own puzzles, with unauthorized copies and imitations became commonplace. The Cube also inspired board games, card games, promotional merchandise, and an extensive assortment of instructional books promising to reveal the secrets of solving it for a meager sum. Its influence extended well beyond the toy industry. The Cube became a fixture of popular culture, appearing in television programs, films, advertisements, cartoons, and comics. Closely associated with the 1980s, it has become a visual symbol of the decade. For some, solving the Cube became an obsessive pastime. Speedcubing developed into a highly competitive international sport, with hopefuls refining techniques to solve the complex puzzles in shorter and shorter times. Advances in technology brought robotic systems into the competition, showing that a handheld toy may serve as a serious challenge in mathematics, engineering, and computer science. This exhibition explores the Rubik’s Cube as both a puzzle and cultural phenomenon, tracing its development, commercial success, numerous offshoots, and continuing influence. From early examples and instructional guides to unusual variations and contemporary speedcubing, the objects presented here illustrate how a deceptively simple invention became a lasting part of popular culture. Few toys are as culturally iconic yet intellectually frustrating as the Rubik’s Cube.

Curated by Stephen Singer and Abigail Traska.

description_text:
Visit the first floor of Bird LIbrary to check out Cube Game: The Rubik's Cube and Other Dimensional Puzzle Games. 

Hungarian Architect and professor of design Ernő Rubik invented the cube in 1974, following his interest in three-dimensional geometry and the relationship between dimensional shapes. Originally known as the Magic Cube, it was rebranded as the Rubik’s Cube upon its worldwide release in 1980, quickly becoming the trendy must-have novelty of the decade. By the early 1980s, millions were attempting to solve its not-so simple challenge: arranging six faces of colored squares so that each displayed a single color. The Cube’s breakout success generated an entire industry of related products. Variations on the original design appeared in numerous shapes, sizes, and configurations, while other mechanical puzzles, including Rubik’s Snake, offered unique ways to manipulate geometric forms. Competing manufacturers introduced their own puzzles, with unauthorized copies and imitations became commonplace. The Cube also inspired board games, card games, promotional merchandise, and an extensive assortment of instructional books promising to reveal the secrets of solving it for a meager sum. Its influence extended well beyond the toy industry. The Cube became a fixture of popular culture, appearing in television programs, films, advertisements, cartoons, and comics. Closely associated with the 1980s, it has become a visual symbol of the decade. For some, solving the Cube became an obsessive pastime. Speedcubing developed into a highly competitive international sport, with hopefuls refining techniques to solve the complex puzzles in shorter and shorter times. Advances in technology brought robotic systems into the competition, showing that a handheld toy may serve as a serious challenge in mathematics, engineering, and computer science. This exhibition explores the Rubik’s Cube as both a puzzle and cultural phenomenon, tracing its development, commercial success, numerous offshoots, and continuing influence. From early examples and instructional guides to unusual variations and contemporary speedcubing, the objects presented here illustrate how a deceptively simple invention became a lasting part of popular culture. Few toys are as culturally iconic yet intellectually frustrating as the Rubik’s Cube.

Curated by Stephen Singer and Abigail Traska.

title: Reclaimed: The Art of Recology
description:
September 1 - December 11, 2026

Reclaimed: The Art of Recology presents a survey of 33 artists who were selected to participate in Recology’s Artist-in-Residence program, which began in 1990. Armed with safety gear and a shopping cart, each of these artists have scavenging privileges in the Public Reuse and Recycling Area—what most artists refer to as “The Big Store”—to recycle and reclaim the discarded waste as imagined art objects. Through introspective, playful, and highly original explorations, the artists reveal the hidden stories our rubbish tells us about our complex relationship with the world, while highlighting the need to create sustainable communities.

This exhibition is curated by Emilee Enders. The exhibition tour is organized by Bedford Gallery at the Lesher Center for the Arts, Walnut Creek, CA.

description:
August 25 - December 11, 2026

Between the 1940s and his death in 1993, the printmaker Letterio Calapai produced dozens of works about outer space and Catholic subjects. This exhibition examines how his art transformed as these subjects evolved during his lifetime and reveals how one man understood the changing world around him.

This exhibition was curated by Julia Neufeld G’23 G’24. We gratefully acknowledge the Dryer Family Foundation for supporting this project.
