The Maxwell School will be the inaugural host of the traveling exhibit “The Promise of Public Service” curated by the National Academy of Public Administration and showcasing public servants at all levels from across America, past and present.

The traveling exhibit is part of the Academy’s yearlong “Celebration of the American Public Servant,” dedicated to strengthening American democracy and public service as we honor the nation’s 250th anniversary.

The full exhibit was showcased at the Library of Congress during the Celebration of the American Public Servant 250 Gala in June, with the traveling exhibit on display in the Maxwell Hall foyer through the fall semester.

title: SCRC Exhibition "We Demand! A Legacy of Activism in America"
description:
Since the country’s founding, the American people have shaped—and continue to shape—a more just and equitable future for current and future generations. For decades, Syracuse University Libraries’ Special Collections Research Center (SCRC) has collected materials related to histories of activism and social reform in America that illustrate how advancements in rights were made possible by those who came before. This tireless pursuit and ongoing work of individuals and collective groups who have come together to push for change—not always seen during their lifetimes—in the face of extraordinary challenges and circumstances is documented within this exhibition.

Visitors can explore traces of resistance and perseverance in the form of publications, posters, protest signs, photographs, demands, newsletters, and more that document the critical role of activism in challenging injustice and securing greater freedoms for all.

The exhibition was curated by Courtney Hicks, SCRC Lead Curator and Curator of Plastics and Historical Artifacts, Jana Rosinski, SCRC Instruction and Education Librarian, and Lindy Smith, SCRC Assistant Director.

title: Exit Strategies
address: 945 Chung King Rd., Los Angeles, CA 90012
description:
“Exit Strategies” brings together the work of Melanie Bisbach, Danielle Chandler and A.J. Miller, three artists whose sculptures and installations offer plans of escape in a chaotic world and trace the echoes of an absent subject.

Each artist uses craft-based techniques and materials, exploring new coping mechanisms for the stressful environments in which they live. Bisbach’s porcelain sculptures isolate botanical forms from the living things the works describe, fixing blades of grass in permanence to be read. Chandler’s ceramic and textile works construct inner architectures. Her installation invites visitors to enter for a time, to be vulnerable and to choose what to guard and what to reveal. Similarly, Miller’s commentary on domestic craft treats the hobby as a fragile form of leisure in an uncertain economy.

“Exit Strategies” constructs a threshold that allows viewers to find themselves outside their reality.

The exhibition will be on view Nov. 6-22. An opening will be held on Friday, Nov. 6, from 6-9 p.m. The gallery is open Fridays and Saturdays from noon to 6 p.m. and by appointment.

title: Talking to Our Tech
description:
“Talking to Our Tech” presents works by students in Media Art and Critique (CRS 360) exploring the intersections of contemporary art, artificial intelligence and new media practices. Bringing together students with varied levels of experience in media arts and technology, the exhibition reflects a semester of experimentation with computer vision, machine listening and image generation techniques. 

At the center of this exhibition is a conversation between the maker and the machine and between the artwork and the viewer. These exchanges invite us to consider how technology participates in creative processes, influences mediation and rewires our relationship to images and information. They reveal the possibilities, complications and unexpected discoveries that emerge when we learn to talk to our tech. 

On View: Friday, Nov. 20, 2026 - Friday, Jan. 15, 2027
Reception: Friday, Dec. 4, from 5:30 – 7:30 p.m.

title: Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering Graduate Seminar: Extreme Aerodynamics: Beyond the Envelope
description:
Speaker: Dr. Kunihiko (Sam) Taira, Professor at University of California, Los Angeles 

Title: Extreme Aerodynamics: Beyond the Envelope

Abstract Summary:

This talk examines flight in extreme aerodynamic conditions—such as the turbulent wakes of urban canyons, mountainous terrain, and ships—that pose severe challenges for small-scale aircraft due to large gust disturbances occurring on timescales comparable to flow instabilities. Using computational and physics-embedded machine learning methods, Dr. Taira’s group has found that these extreme flows are surprisingly low-dimensional with similarities across a wide range of Reynolds numbers, enabling the development of fast-acting flow control and optimal wing designs to suppress transient loads.

title: Jumuah Prayer
description:
In Islam, Friday prayer, or Congregational prayer (Arabic: صَلَاة ٱلْجُمُعَة Ṣalāt al-Jumuʿah), is a prayer (ṣalāt) that Muslims hold every Friday after noon, instead of the Zuhr prayer. Muslims ordinarily pray five times each day according to the sun's sky path, regardless of time zones. Youm Jumu’ah ("day of congregation"), or simply Jumuah means Friday in Arabic. In many Muslim countries, the weekend is inclusive of Fridays, and in others, Fridays are half-days for schools and some workplaces. It is one of the most exalted Islamic rituals and one of its confirmed obligatory acts.  

Muslim Student Life at Syracuse University supports Muslim students, faculty, and staff in all religious and spiritual needs for development and growth. It is about accommodation, openness, and understanding – not judgement or restriction. Muslim Student Life aims at improving understanding and representation of Muslim cultures and communities here in the US and around the world through sharing our universal values with people of faith and no faith. 

For more information, please check Hendricks Chapel’s Muslim Student Life web page.

title: Henry V
description:
By William Shakespeare | Directed by John Tufts

Nov. 13 – 21 | Opening Night: Nov. 14

Pressed by powerful nobles and church leaders to reclaim England’s sovereignty over France, the young, rebellious King Henry V of England raises an army and carves his way to Agincourt, where his troops, depleted and exhausted, must face the enemy head-on. But with dissension in the ranks, Henry will have to prove himself a strong and legitimate ruler if he’s to inspire his men to lay down their lives for their country and their king. Shakespeare’s thrilling history play ponders the true cost of winning in the epic game of thrones.

title: Bird Library Exhibition: Cube Game
description:
Visit the first floor of Bird LIbrary to check out Cube Game: The Rubik's Cube and Other Dimensional Puzzle Games. 

Hungarian Architect and professor of design Ernő Rubik invented the cube in 1974, following his interest in three-dimensional geometry and the relationship between dimensional shapes. Originally known as the Magic Cube, it was rebranded as the Rubik’s Cube upon its worldwide release in 1980, quickly becoming the trendy must-have novelty of the decade. By the early 1980s, millions were attempting to solve its not-so simple challenge: arranging six faces of colored squares so that each displayed a single color. The Cube’s breakout success generated an entire industry of related products. Variations on the original design appeared in numerous shapes, sizes, and configurations, while other mechanical puzzles, including Rubik’s Snake, offered unique ways to manipulate geometric forms. Competing manufacturers introduced their own puzzles, with unauthorized copies and imitations became commonplace. The Cube also inspired board games, card games, promotional merchandise, and an extensive assortment of instructional books promising to reveal the secrets of solving it for a meager sum. Its influence extended well beyond the toy industry. The Cube became a fixture of popular culture, appearing in television programs, films, advertisements, cartoons, and comics. Closely associated with the 1980s, it has become a visual symbol of the decade. For some, solving the Cube became an obsessive pastime. Speedcubing developed into a highly competitive international sport, with hopefuls refining techniques to solve the complex puzzles in shorter and shorter times. Advances in technology brought robotic systems into the competition, showing that a handheld toy may serve as a serious challenge in mathematics, engineering, and computer science. This exhibition explores the Rubik’s Cube as both a puzzle and cultural phenomenon, tracing its development, commercial success, numerous offshoots, and continuing influence. From early examples and instructional guides to unusual variations and contemporary speedcubing, the objects presented here illustrate how a deceptively simple invention became a lasting part of popular culture. Few toys are as culturally iconic yet intellectually frustrating as the Rubik’s Cube.

Curated by Stephen Singer and Abigail Traska.

Game On!: Titles from the Bird Library Board Game Collection featured in the Miron case.

What do the Sheriff of Nottingham, the pandemic and exploding kittens have in common? They're all subjects of board and card games from Bird Library's game collection, located in the first-floor Learning Commons. Whether you're looking to do a puzzle, topple a Jenga tower or take a Risk, we have them all, free to borrow!

title: Class of 2028 Senior Class Marshal Applications
description:
Calling all juniors! Apply to be the Class of 2028 Senior Class Marshals.

Senior Class Marshals are Syracuse University's most committed and thoughtful students. They are distinguished individuals who exemplify the spirit of the senior class, embody One University, exhibit academic excellence and have excelled during their time at Syracuse. Each year, two Syracuse University rising seniors will be selected to serve as the all-University student representatives for their graduating class. During their senior year, they will have unique opportunities to engage with various University stakeholders, help select their Commencement speaker and discuss their student experience and offer constructive suggestions with senior administrators.

The deadline to apply is Friday, Jan. 15, 2027, 11:59 p.m.

Referrals

If you would like to refer a student for Senior Class Marshal and understand the requirements and expectations, please submit the reference form.

title: Family Support Navigator Applications
description:
Family Support Navigators (FSNs) serve as a vital resource and support system for parents, families and supporters of students enrolled at Syracuse University. This is a paid position for undergraduate students at Syracuse University, providing support during Summer Family/Supporter Orientation.

Students interested in becoming a Family Support Navigator must meet the following qualifications.

  • Be a full-time Syracuse University undergraduate student.
  • Maintain a cumulative GPA of at least 2.5.
  • Must give permission to verify good standing through Community Standards.
  • Must be on campus for the Spring 2027 semester.
  • Must be able to attend necessary trainings and events.
  • Have no work or co-curricular conflicts during any of the orientation session dates.

Family Support Navigator applications are due Sunday, Nov. 22. Interested students should apply online.

description:
August 25 - May 8, 2027

For the sixth iteration of The Art Wall Project, Helen Zughaib ’81 uses her characteristic bright color palette and intricate patterns to explore the stories of people’s displacement from their homes. By painting migration narratives from her own family’s history and our contemporary experiences, Zughaib considers how this global movement of individuals has shaped America as we know it today.

title: Reclaimed: The Art of Recology
description:
September 1 - December 11, 2026

Reclaimed: The Art of Recology presents a survey of 33 artists who were selected to participate in Recology’s Artist-in-Residence program, which began in 1990. Armed with safety gear and a shopping cart, each of these artists have scavenging privileges in the Public Reuse and Recycling Area—what most artists refer to as “The Big Store”—to recycle and reclaim the discarded waste as imagined art objects. Through introspective, playful, and highly original explorations, the artists reveal the hidden stories our rubbish tells us about our complex relationship with the world, while highlighting the need to create sustainable communities.

This exhibition is curated by Emilee Enders. The exhibition tour is organized by Bedford Gallery at the Lesher Center for the Arts, Walnut Creek, CA.

title: Space and the Sacred: Letterio Calapai's Prints
description:
August 25 - December 11, 2026

Between the 1940s and his death in 1993, the printmaker Letterio Calapai produced dozens of works about outer space and Catholic subjects. This exhibition examines how his art transformed as these subjects evolved during his lifetime and reveals how one man understood the changing world around him.

This exhibition was curated by Julia Neufeld G’23 G’24. We gratefully acknowledge the Dryer Family Foundation for supporting this project.

description:
The Maxwell School will be the inaugural host of the traveling exhibit “The Promise of Public Service” curated by the National Academy of Public Administration and showcasing public servants at all levels from across America, past and present.

The traveling exhibit is part of the Academy’s yearlong “Celebration of the American Public Servant,” dedicated to strengthening American democracy and public service as we honor the nation’s 250th anniversary.

The full exhibit was showcased at the Library of Congress during the Celebration of the American Public Servant 250 Gala in June, with the traveling exhibit on display in the Maxwell Hall foyer through the fall semester.

title: Exit Strategies
address: 945 Chung King Rd., Los Angeles, CA 90012
description:
“Exit Strategies” brings together the work of Melanie Bisbach, Danielle Chandler and A.J. Miller, three artists whose sculptures and installations offer plans of escape in a chaotic world and trace the echoes of an absent subject.

Each artist uses craft-based techniques and materials, exploring new coping mechanisms for the stressful environments in which they live. Bisbach’s porcelain sculptures isolate botanical forms from the living things the works describe, fixing blades of grass in permanence to be read. Chandler’s ceramic and textile works construct inner architectures. Her installation invites visitors to enter for a time, to be vulnerable and to choose what to guard and what to reveal. Similarly, Miller’s commentary on domestic craft treats the hobby as a fragile form of leisure in an uncertain economy.

“Exit Strategies” constructs a threshold that allows viewers to find themselves outside their reality.

The exhibition will be on view Nov. 6-22. An opening will be held on Friday, Nov. 6, from 6-9 p.m. The gallery is open Fridays and Saturdays from noon to 6 p.m. and by appointment.

The exhibition will be on view Nov. 6-22. An opening will be held on Friday, Nov. 6, from 6-9 p.m. The gallery is open Fridays and Saturdays from noon to 6 p.m. and by appointment.

title: Talking to Our Tech
description:
“Talking to Our Tech” presents works by students in Media Art and Critique (CRS 360) exploring the intersections of contemporary art, artificial intelligence and new media practices. Bringing together students with varied levels of experience in media arts and technology, the exhibition reflects a semester of experimentation with computer vision, machine listening and image generation techniques. 

At the center of this exhibition is a conversation between the maker and the machine and between the artwork and the viewer. These exchanges invite us to consider how technology participates in creative processes, influences mediation and rewires our relationship to images and information. They reveal the possibilities, complications and unexpected discoveries that emerge when we learn to talk to our tech. 

On View: Friday, Nov. 20, 2026 - Friday, Jan. 15, 2027
Reception: Friday, Dec. 4, from 5:30 – 7:30 p.m.

description:
By William Shakespeare | Directed by John Tufts

Nov. 13 – 21 | Opening Night: Nov. 14

Pressed by powerful nobles and church leaders to reclaim England’s sovereignty over France, the young, rebellious King Henry V of England raises an army and carves his way to Agincourt, where his troops, depleted and exhausted, must face the enemy head-on. But with dissension in the ranks, Henry will have to prove himself a strong and legitimate ruler if he’s to inspire his men to lay down their lives for their country and their king. Shakespeare’s thrilling history play ponders the true cost of winning in the epic game of thrones.

title: Bird Library Exhibition: Cube Game
description:
Visit the first floor of Bird LIbrary to check out Cube Game: The Rubik's Cube and Other Dimensional Puzzle Games. 

Hungarian Architect and professor of design Ernő Rubik invented the cube in 1974, following his interest in three-dimensional geometry and the relationship between dimensional shapes. Originally known as the Magic Cube, it was rebranded as the Rubik’s Cube upon its worldwide release in 1980, quickly becoming the trendy must-have novelty of the decade. By the early 1980s, millions were attempting to solve its not-so simple challenge: arranging six faces of colored squares so that each displayed a single color. The Cube’s breakout success generated an entire industry of related products. Variations on the original design appeared in numerous shapes, sizes, and configurations, while other mechanical puzzles, including Rubik’s Snake, offered unique ways to manipulate geometric forms. Competing manufacturers introduced their own puzzles, with unauthorized copies and imitations became commonplace. The Cube also inspired board games, card games, promotional merchandise, and an extensive assortment of instructional books promising to reveal the secrets of solving it for a meager sum. Its influence extended well beyond the toy industry. The Cube became a fixture of popular culture, appearing in television programs, films, advertisements, cartoons, and comics. Closely associated with the 1980s, it has become a visual symbol of the decade. For some, solving the Cube became an obsessive pastime. Speedcubing developed into a highly competitive international sport, with hopefuls refining techniques to solve the complex puzzles in shorter and shorter times. Advances in technology brought robotic systems into the competition, showing that a handheld toy may serve as a serious challenge in mathematics, engineering, and computer science. This exhibition explores the Rubik’s Cube as both a puzzle and cultural phenomenon, tracing its development, commercial success, numerous offshoots, and continuing influence. From early examples and instructional guides to unusual variations and contemporary speedcubing, the objects presented here illustrate how a deceptively simple invention became a lasting part of popular culture. Few toys are as culturally iconic yet intellectually frustrating as the Rubik’s Cube.

Curated by Stephen Singer and Abigail Traska.

Game On!: Titles from the Bird Library Board Game Collection featured in the Miron case.

What do the Sheriff of Nottingham, the pandemic and exploding kittens have in common? They're all subjects of board and card games from Bird Library's game collection, located in the first-floor Learning Commons. Whether you're looking to do a puzzle, topple a Jenga tower or take a Risk, we have them all, free to borrow!

Senior Class Marshals are Syracuse University's most committed and thoughtful students. description:
Family Support Navigators (FSNs) serve as a vital resource and support system for parents, families and supporters of students enrolled at Syracuse University. This is a paid position for undergraduate students at Syracuse University, providing support during Summer Family/Supporter Orientation.

Students interested in becoming a Family Support Navigator must meet the following qualifications.

  • Be a full-time Syracuse University undergraduate student.
  • Maintain a cumulative GPA of at least 2.5.
  • Must give permission to verify good standing through Community Standards.
  • Must be on campus for the Spring 2027 semester.
  • Must be able to attend necessary trainings and events.
  • Have no work or co-curricular conflicts during any of the orientation session dates.

Family Support Navigator applications are due Sunday, Nov. 22. Interested students should apply online.

description:
August 25 - May 8, 2027

For the sixth iteration of The Art Wall Project, Helen Zughaib ’81 uses her characteristic bright color palette and intricate patterns to explore the stories of people’s displacement from their homes. By painting migration narratives from her own family’s history and our contemporary experiences, Zughaib considers how this global movement of individuals has shaped America as we know it today.

title: Reclaimed: The Art of Recology
description:
September 1 - December 11, 2026

Reclaimed: The Art of Recology presents a survey of 33 artists who were selected to participate in Recology’s Artist-in-Residence program, which began in 1990. Armed with safety gear and a shopping cart, each of these artists have scavenging privileges in the Public Reuse and Recycling Area—what most artists refer to as “The Big Store”—to recycle and reclaim the discarded waste as imagined art objects. Through introspective, playful, and highly original explorations, the artists reveal the hidden stories our rubbish tells us about our complex relationship with the world, while highlighting the need to create sustainable communities.

This exhibition is curated by Emilee Enders. The exhibition tour is organized by Bedford Gallery at the Lesher Center for the Arts, Walnut Creek, CA.

title: Space and the Sacred: Letterio Calapai's Prints
description:
August 25 - December 11, 2026

Between the 1940s and his death in 1993, the printmaker Letterio Calapai produced dozens of works about outer space and Catholic subjects. This exhibition examines how his art transformed as these subjects evolved during his lifetime and reveals how one man understood the changing world around him.

This exhibition was curated by Julia Neufeld G’23 G’24. We gratefully acknowledge the Dryer Family Foundation for supporting this project.

title: The Promise of Public Service Exhibit
description:
The Maxwell School will be the inaugural host of the traveling exhibit “The Promise of Public Service” curated by the National Academy of Public Administration and showcasing public servants at all levels from across America, past and present.

The traveling exhibit is part of the Academy’s yearlong “Celebration of the American Public Servant,” dedicated to strengthening American democracy and public service as we honor the nation’s 250th anniversary.

The full exhibit was showcased at the Library of Congress during the Celebration of the American Public Servant 250 Gala in June, with the traveling exhibit on display in the Maxwell Hall foyer through the fall semester.

title: Bird Library Exhibition: Cube Game
description:
Visit the first floor of Bird LIbrary to check out Cube Game: The Rubik's Cube and Other Dimensional Puzzle Games. 

Hungarian Architect and professor of design Ernő Rubik invented the cube in 1974, following his interest in three-dimensional geometry and the relationship between dimensional shapes. Originally known as the Magic Cube, it was rebranded as the Rubik’s Cube upon its worldwide release in 1980, quickly becoming the trendy must-have novelty of the decade. By the early 1980s, millions were attempting to solve its not-so simple challenge: arranging six faces of colored squares so that each displayed a single color. The Cube’s breakout success generated an entire industry of related products. Variations on the original design appeared in numerous shapes, sizes, and configurations, while other mechanical puzzles, including Rubik’s Snake, offered unique ways to manipulate geometric forms. Competing manufacturers introduced their own puzzles, with unauthorized copies and imitations became commonplace. The Cube also inspired board games, card games, promotional merchandise, and an extensive assortment of instructional books promising to reveal the secrets of solving it for a meager sum. Its influence extended well beyond the toy industry. The Cube became a fixture of popular culture, appearing in television programs, films, advertisements, cartoons, and comics. Closely associated with the 1980s, it has become a visual symbol of the decade. For some, solving the Cube became an obsessive pastime. Speedcubing developed into a highly competitive international sport, with hopefuls refining techniques to solve the complex puzzles in shorter and shorter times. Advances in technology brought robotic systems into the competition, showing that a handheld toy may serve as a serious challenge in mathematics, engineering, and computer science. This exhibition explores the Rubik’s Cube as both a puzzle and cultural phenomenon, tracing its development, commercial success, numerous offshoots, and continuing influence. From early examples and instructional guides to unusual variations and contemporary speedcubing, the objects presented here illustrate how a deceptively simple invention became a lasting part of popular culture. Few toys are as culturally iconic yet intellectually frustrating as the Rubik’s Cube.

Curated by Stephen Singer and Abigail Traska.

What do the Sheriff of Nottingham, the pandemic and exploding kittens have in common? They're all subjects of board and card games from Bird Library's game collection, located in the first-floor Learning Commons. Whether you're looking to do a puzzle, topple a Jenga tower or take a Risk, we have them all, free to borrow!

Senior Class Marshals are Syracuse University's most committed and thoughtful students. title: Helen Zughaib: Patterns of Migration
description:
August 25 - May 8, 2027

For the sixth iteration of The Art Wall Project, Helen Zughaib ’81 uses her characteristic bright color palette and intricate patterns to explore the stories of people’s displacement from their homes. By painting migration narratives from her own family’s history and our contemporary experiences, Zughaib considers how this global movement of individuals has shaped America as we know it today.

description:
The Mark and Pearle Clements Internship Awards are intended to enable Syracuse University students to undertake unique summer internships that they have developed on their own initiative and that would not be possible to undertake without financial help. The objective is that students create their own internship, working under the guidance and supervision of an experienced professional who can help them explore opportunities that link theory with practice in their fields of career interest.

Eligibility

  • Syracuse University juniors and master’s degree students of all majors are eligible to apply.
  • Academic credit may be earned for participation in these internships, but is not required.

Please contact Student Employment and Internship Support at cuseworks@syr.edu with questions or for more information.

title: Reclaimed: The Art of Recology
description:
September 1 - December 11, 2026

Reclaimed: The Art of Recology presents a survey of 33 artists who were selected to participate in Recology’s Artist-in-Residence program, which began in 1990. Armed with safety gear and a shopping cart, each of these artists have scavenging privileges in the Public Reuse and Recycling Area—what most artists refer to as “The Big Store”—to recycle and reclaim the discarded waste as imagined art objects. Through introspective, playful, and highly original explorations, the artists reveal the hidden stories our rubbish tells us about our complex relationship with the world, while highlighting the need to create sustainable communities.

This exhibition is curated by Emilee Enders. The exhibition tour is organized by Bedford Gallery at the Lesher Center for the Arts, Walnut Creek, CA.

title: Space and the Sacred: Letterio Calapai's Prints
description:
August 25 - December 11, 2026

Between the 1940s and his death in 1993, the printmaker Letterio Calapai produced dozens of works about outer space and Catholic subjects. This exhibition examines how his art transformed as these subjects evolved during his lifetime and reveals how one man understood the changing world around him.

This exhibition was curated by Julia Neufeld G’23 G’24. We gratefully acknowledge the Dryer Family Foundation for supporting this project.

title: The Promise of Public Service Exhibit
description:
The Maxwell School will be the inaugural host of the traveling exhibit “The Promise of Public Service” curated by the National Academy of Public Administration and showcasing public servants at all levels from across America, past and present.

The traveling exhibit is part of the Academy’s yearlong “Celebration of the American Public Servant,” dedicated to strengthening American democracy and public service as we honor the nation’s 250th anniversary.

The full exhibit was showcased at the Library of Congress during the Celebration of the American Public Servant 250 Gala in June, with the traveling exhibit on display in the Maxwell Hall foyer through the fall semester.

title: SCRC Exhibition "We Demand! A Legacy of Activism in America"
description:
Since the country’s founding, the American people have shaped—and continue to shape—a more just and equitable future for current and future generations. For decades, Syracuse University Libraries’ Special Collections Research Center (SCRC) has collected materials related to histories of activism and social reform in America that illustrate how advancements in rights were made possible by those who came before. This tireless pursuit and ongoing work of individuals and collective groups who have come together to push for change—not always seen during their lifetimes—in the face of extraordinary challenges and circumstances is documented within this exhibition.

Visitors can explore traces of resistance and perseverance in the form of publications, posters, protest signs, photographs, demands, newsletters, and more that document the critical role of activism in challenging injustice and securing greater freedoms for all.

The exhibition was curated by Courtney Hicks, SCRC Lead Curator and Curator of Plastics and Historical Artifacts, Jana Rosinski, SCRC Instruction and Education Librarian, and Lindy Smith, SCRC Assistant Director.

title: Reclaimed: The Art of Recology
description:
September 1 - December 11, 2026

Reclaimed: The Art of Recology presents a survey of 33 artists who were selected to participate in Recology’s Artist-in-Residence program, which began in 1990. Armed with safety gear and a shopping cart, each of these artists have scavenging privileges in the Public Reuse and Recycling Area—what most artists refer to as “The Big Store”—to recycle and reclaim the discarded waste as imagined art objects. Through introspective, playful, and highly original explorations, the artists reveal the hidden stories our rubbish tells us about our complex relationship with the world, while highlighting the need to create sustainable communities.

This exhibition is curated by Emilee Enders. The exhibition tour is organized by Bedford Gallery at the Lesher Center for the Arts, Walnut Creek, CA.

title: Space and the Sacred: Letterio Calapai's Prints
description:
August 25 - December 11, 2026

Between the 1940s and his death in 1993, the printmaker Letterio Calapai produced dozens of works about outer space and Catholic subjects. This exhibition examines how his art transformed as these subjects evolved during his lifetime and reveals how one man understood the changing world around him.

This exhibition was curated by Julia Neufeld G’23 G’24. We gratefully acknowledge the Dryer Family Foundation for supporting this project.

The full exhibit was showcased at the Library of Congress during the Celebration of the American Public Servant 250 Gala in June, with the traveling exhibit on display in the Maxwell Hall foyer through the fall semester.

title: SCRC Exhibition "We Demand! A Legacy of Activism in America"
description:
Since the country’s founding, the American people have shaped—and continue to shape—a more just and equitable future for current and future generations. For decades, Syracuse University Libraries’ Special Collections Research Center (SCRC) has collected materials related to histories of activism and social reform in America that illustrate how advancements in rights were made possible by those who came before. This tireless pursuit and ongoing work of individuals and collective groups who have come together to push for change—not always seen during their lifetimes—in the face of extraordinary challenges and circumstances is documented within this exhibition.

Visitors can explore traces of resistance and perseverance in the form of publications, posters, protest signs, photographs, demands, newsletters, and more that document the critical role of activism in challenging injustice and securing greater freedoms for all.

The exhibition was curated by Courtney Hicks, SCRC Lead Curator and Curator of Plastics and Historical Artifacts, Jana Rosinski, SCRC Instruction and Education Librarian, and Lindy Smith, SCRC Assistant Director.

title: Talking to Our Tech
description:
“Talking to Our Tech” presents works by students in Media Art and Critique (CRS 360) exploring the intersections of contemporary art, artificial intelligence and new media practices. Bringing together students with varied levels of experience in media arts and technology, the exhibition reflects a semester of experimentation with computer vision, machine listening and image generation techniques. 

At the center of this exhibition is a conversation between the maker and the machine and between the artwork and the viewer. These exchanges invite us to consider how technology participates in creative processes, influences mediation and rewires our relationship to images and information. They reveal the possibilities, complications and unexpected discoveries that emerge when we learn to talk to our tech. 

On View: Friday, Nov. 20, 2026 - Friday, Jan. 15, 2027
Reception: Friday, Dec. 4, from 5:30 – 7:30 p.m.

title: Bird Library Exhibition: Cube Game
description:
Visit the first floor of Bird LIbrary to check out Cube Game: The Rubik's Cube and Other Dimensional Puzzle Games. 

Hungarian Architect and professor of design Ernő Rubik invented the cube in 1974, following his interest in three-dimensional geometry and the relationship between dimensional shapes. Originally known as the Magic Cube, it was rebranded as the Rubik’s Cube upon its worldwide release in 1980, quickly becoming the trendy must-have novelty of the decade. By the early 1980s, millions were attempting to solve its not-so simple challenge: arranging six faces of colored squares so that each displayed a single color. The Cube’s breakout success generated an entire industry of related products. Variations on the original design appeared in numerous shapes, sizes, and configurations, while other mechanical puzzles, including Rubik’s Snake, offered unique ways to manipulate geometric forms. Competing manufacturers introduced their own puzzles, with unauthorized copies and imitations became commonplace. The Cube also inspired board games, card games, promotional merchandise, and an extensive assortment of instructional books promising to reveal the secrets of solving it for a meager sum. Its influence extended well beyond the toy industry. The Cube became a fixture of popular culture, appearing in television programs, films, advertisements, cartoons, and comics. Closely associated with the 1980s, it has become a visual symbol of the decade. For some, solving the Cube became an obsessive pastime. Speedcubing developed into a highly competitive international sport, with hopefuls refining techniques to solve the complex puzzles in shorter and shorter times. Advances in technology brought robotic systems into the competition, showing that a handheld toy may serve as a serious challenge in mathematics, engineering, and computer science. This exhibition explores the Rubik’s Cube as both a puzzle and cultural phenomenon, tracing its development, commercial success, numerous offshoots, and continuing influence. From early examples and instructional guides to unusual variations and contemporary speedcubing, the objects presented here illustrate how a deceptively simple invention became a lasting part of popular culture. Few toys are as culturally iconic yet intellectually frustrating as the Rubik’s Cube.

Curated by Stephen Singer and Abigail Traska.

Game On!: Titles from the Bird Library Board Game Collection featured in the Miron case.

What do the Sheriff of Nottingham, the pandemic and exploding kittens have in common? They're all subjects of board and card games from Bird Library's game collection, located in the first-floor Learning Commons. Whether you're looking to do a puzzle, topple a Jenga tower or take a Risk, we have them all, free to borrow!

title: Class of 2028 Senior Class Marshal Applications
description:
Calling all juniors! Apply to be the Class of 2028 Senior Class Marshals.

Senior Class Marshals are Syracuse University's most committed and thoughtful students. They are distinguished individuals who exemplify the spirit of the senior class, embody One University, exhibit academic excellence and have excelled during their time at Syracuse. Each year, two Syracuse University rising seniors will be selected to serve as the all-University student representatives for their graduating class. During their senior year, they will have unique opportunities to engage with various University stakeholders, help select their Commencement speaker and discuss their student experience and offer constructive suggestions with senior administrators.

Referrals

title: SCRC Exhibition "We Demand! A Legacy of Activism in America"
description:
Since the country’s founding, the American people have shaped—and continue to shape—a more just and equitable future for current and future generations. For decades, Syracuse University Libraries’ Special Collections Research Center (SCRC) has collected materials related to histories of activism and social reform in America that illustrate how advancements in rights were made possible by those who came before. This tireless pursuit and ongoing work of individuals and collective groups who have come together to push for change—not always seen during their lifetimes—in the face of extraordinary challenges and circumstances is documented within this exhibition.

Visitors can explore traces of resistance and perseverance in the form of publications, posters, protest signs, photographs, demands, newsletters, and more that document the critical role of activism in challenging injustice and securing greater freedoms for all.

The exhibition was curated by Courtney Hicks, SCRC Lead Curator and Curator of Plastics and Historical Artifacts, Jana Rosinski, SCRC Instruction and Education Librarian, and Lindy Smith, SCRC Assistant Director.

title: Talking to Our Tech
description:
“Talking to Our Tech” presents works by students in Media Art and Critique (CRS 360) exploring the intersections of contemporary art, artificial intelligence and new media practices. Bringing together students with varied levels of experience in media arts and technology, the exhibition reflects a semester of experimentation with computer vision, machine listening and image generation techniques. 

At the center of this exhibition is a conversation between the maker and the machine and between the artwork and the viewer. These exchanges invite us to consider how technology participates in creative processes, influences mediation and rewires our relationship to images and information. They reveal the possibilities, complications and unexpected discoveries that emerge when we learn to talk to our tech. 

On View: Friday, Nov. 20, 2026 - Friday, Jan. 15, 2027
Reception: Friday, Dec. 4, from 5:30 – 7:30 p.m.

title: Bird Library Exhibition: Cube Game
description:
Visit the first floor of Bird LIbrary to check out Cube Game: The Rubik's Cube and Other Dimensional Puzzle Games. 

Hungarian Architect and professor of design Ernő Rubik invented the cube in 1974, following his interest in three-dimensional geometry and the relationship between dimensional shapes. Originally known as the Magic Cube, it was rebranded as the Rubik’s Cube upon its worldwide release in 1980, quickly becoming the trendy must-have novelty of the decade. By the early 1980s, millions were attempting to solve its not-so simple challenge: arranging six faces of colored squares so that each displayed a single color. The Cube’s breakout success generated an entire industry of related products. Variations on the original design appeared in numerous shapes, sizes, and configurations, while other mechanical puzzles, including Rubik’s Snake, offered unique ways to manipulate geometric forms. Competing manufacturers introduced their own puzzles, with unauthorized copies and imitations became commonplace. The Cube also inspired board games, card games, promotional merchandise, and an extensive assortment of instructional books promising to reveal the secrets of solving it for a meager sum. Its influence extended well beyond the toy industry. The Cube became a fixture of popular culture, appearing in television programs, films, advertisements, cartoons, and comics. Closely associated with the 1980s, it has become a visual symbol of the decade. For some, solving the Cube became an obsessive pastime. Speedcubing developed into a highly competitive international sport, with hopefuls refining techniques to solve the complex puzzles in shorter and shorter times. Advances in technology brought robotic systems into the competition, showing that a handheld toy may serve as a serious challenge in mathematics, engineering, and computer science. This exhibition explores the Rubik’s Cube as both a puzzle and cultural phenomenon, tracing its development, commercial success, numerous offshoots, and continuing influence. From early examples and instructional guides to unusual variations and contemporary speedcubing, the objects presented here illustrate how a deceptively simple invention became a lasting part of popular culture. Few toys are as culturally iconic yet intellectually frustrating as the Rubik’s Cube.

Curated by Stephen Singer and Abigail Traska.

Game On!: Titles from the Bird Library Board Game Collection featured in the Miron case.

What do the Sheriff of Nottingham, the pandemic and exploding kittens have in common? They're all subjects of board and card games from Bird Library's game collection, located in the first-floor Learning Commons. Whether you're looking to do a puzzle, topple a Jenga tower or take a Risk, we have them all, free to borrow!

description:
Calling all juniors! Apply to be the Class of 2028 Senior Class Marshals.

Senior Class Marshals are Syracuse University's most committed and thoughtful students. They are distinguished individuals who exemplify the spirit of the senior class, embody One University, exhibit academic excellence and have excelled during their time at Syracuse. Each year, two Syracuse University rising seniors will be selected to serve as the all-University student representatives for their graduating class. During their senior year, they will have unique opportunities to engage with various University stakeholders, help select their Commencement speaker and discuss their student experience and offer constructive suggestions with senior administrators.

Referrals

title: SCRC Exhibition "We Demand! A Legacy of Activism in America"
description:
Since the country’s founding, the American people have shaped—and continue to shape—a more just and equitable future for current and future generations. For decades, Syracuse University Libraries’ Special Collections Research Center (SCRC) has collected materials related to histories of activism and social reform in America that illustrate how advancements in rights were made possible by those who came before. This tireless pursuit and ongoing work of individuals and collective groups who have come together to push for change—not always seen during their lifetimes—in the face of extraordinary challenges and circumstances is documented within this exhibition.

Visitors can explore traces of resistance and perseverance in the form of publications, posters, protest signs, photographs, demands, newsletters, and more that document the critical role of activism in challenging injustice and securing greater freedoms for all.

The exhibition was curated by Courtney Hicks, SCRC Lead Curator and Curator of Plastics and Historical Artifacts, Jana Rosinski, SCRC Instruction and Education Librarian, and Lindy Smith, SCRC Assistant Director.

title: Bird Library Exhibition: Cube Game
description:
Visit the first floor of Bird LIbrary to check out Cube Game: The Rubik's Cube and Other Dimensional Puzzle Games. 

Hungarian Architect and professor of design Ernő Rubik invented the cube in 1974, following his interest in three-dimensional geometry and the relationship between dimensional shapes. Originally known as the Magic Cube, it was rebranded as the Rubik’s Cube upon its worldwide release in 1980, quickly becoming the trendy must-have novelty of the decade. By the early 1980s, millions were attempting to solve its not-so simple challenge: arranging six faces of colored squares so that each displayed a single color. The Cube’s breakout success generated an entire industry of related products. Variations on the original design appeared in numerous shapes, sizes, and configurations, while other mechanical puzzles, including Rubik’s Snake, offered unique ways to manipulate geometric forms. Competing manufacturers introduced their own puzzles, with unauthorized copies and imitations became commonplace. The Cube also inspired board games, card games, promotional merchandise, and an extensive assortment of instructional books promising to reveal the secrets of solving it for a meager sum. Its influence extended well beyond the toy industry. The Cube became a fixture of popular culture, appearing in television programs, films, advertisements, cartoons, and comics. Closely associated with the 1980s, it has become a visual symbol of the decade. For some, solving the Cube became an obsessive pastime. Speedcubing developed into a highly competitive international sport, with hopefuls refining techniques to solve the complex puzzles in shorter and shorter times. Advances in technology brought robotic systems into the competition, showing that a handheld toy may serve as a serious challenge in mathematics, engineering, and computer science. This exhibition explores the Rubik’s Cube as both a puzzle and cultural phenomenon, tracing its development, commercial success, numerous offshoots, and continuing influence. From early examples and instructional guides to unusual variations and contemporary speedcubing, the objects presented here illustrate how a deceptively simple invention became a lasting part of popular culture. Few toys are as culturally iconic yet intellectually frustrating as the Rubik’s Cube.

Curated by Stephen Singer and Abigail Traska.

Game On!: Titles from the Bird Library Board Game Collection featured in the Miron case.

What do the Sheriff of Nottingham, the pandemic and exploding kittens have in common? They're all subjects of board and card games from Bird Library's game collection, located in the first-floor Learning Commons. Whether you're looking to do a puzzle, topple a Jenga tower or take a Risk, we have them all, free to borrow!

title: Class of 2028 Senior Class Marshal Applications
description:
Calling all juniors! Apply to be the Class of 2028 Senior Class Marshals.

Senior Class Marshals are Syracuse University's most committed and thoughtful students. They are distinguished individuals who exemplify the spirit of the senior class, embody One University, exhibit academic excellence and have excelled during their time at Syracuse. Each year, two Syracuse University rising seniors will be selected to serve as the all-University student representatives for their graduating class. During their senior year, they will have unique opportunities to engage with various University stakeholders, help select their Commencement speaker and discuss their student experience and offer constructive suggestions with senior administrators.

The deadline to apply is Friday, Jan. 15, 2027, 11:59 p.m.

Referrals

If you would like to refer a student for Senior Class Marshal and understand the requirements and expectations, please submit the reference form.

title: Helen Zughaib: Patterns of Migration
description:
August 25 - May 8, 2027

For the sixth iteration of The Art Wall Project, Helen Zughaib ’81 uses her characteristic bright color palette and intricate patterns to explore the stories of people’s displacement from their homes. By painting migration narratives from her own family’s history and our contemporary experiences, Zughaib considers how this global movement of individuals has shaped America as we know it today.

title: Mark and Pearle Clements Internship Award Applications
description:
The Mark and Pearle Clements Internship Awards are intended to enable Syracuse University students to undertake unique summer internships that they have developed on their own initiative and that would not be possible to undertake without financial help. The objective is that students create their own internship, working under the guidance and supervision of an experienced professional who can help them explore opportunities that link theory with practice in their fields of career interest.

Eligibility

  • Syracuse University juniors and master’s degree students of all majors are eligible to apply.
  • Academic credit may be earned for participation in these internships, but is not required.

Please contact Student Employment and Internship Support at cuseworks@syr.edu with questions or for more information.

title: Reclaimed: The Art of Recology
description:
September 1 - December 11, 2026

Reclaimed: The Art of Recology presents a survey of 33 artists who were selected to participate in Recology’s Artist-in-Residence program, which began in 1990. Armed with safety gear and a shopping cart, each of these artists have scavenging privileges in the Public Reuse and Recycling Area—what most artists refer to as “The Big Store”—to recycle and reclaim the discarded waste as imagined art objects. Through introspective, playful, and highly original explorations, the artists reveal the hidden stories our rubbish tells us about our complex relationship with the world, while highlighting the need to create sustainable communities.

This exhibition is curated by Emilee Enders. The exhibition tour is organized by Bedford Gallery at the Lesher Center for the Arts, Walnut Creek, CA.

title: Space and the Sacred: Letterio Calapai's Prints
description:
August 25 - December 11, 2026

Between the 1940s and his death in 1993, the printmaker Letterio Calapai produced dozens of works about outer space and Catholic subjects. This exhibition examines how his art transformed as these subjects evolved during his lifetime and reveals how one man understood the changing world around him.

This exhibition was curated by Julia Neufeld G’23 G’24. We gratefully acknowledge the Dryer Family Foundation for supporting this project.

title: The Promise of Public Service Exhibit
description:
The Maxwell School will be the inaugural host of the traveling exhibit “The Promise of Public Service” curated by the National Academy of Public Administration and showcasing public servants at all levels from across America, past and present.

The traveling exhibit is part of the Academy’s yearlong “Celebration of the American Public Servant,” dedicated to strengthening American democracy and public service as we honor the nation’s 250th anniversary.

The full exhibit was showcased at the Library of Congress during the Celebration of the American Public Servant 250 Gala in June, with the traveling exhibit on display in the Maxwell Hall foyer through the fall semester.

Advances in technology brought robotic systems into the competition, showing that a handheld toy may serve as a serious challenge in mathematics, engineering, and computer science. title: Reclaimed: The Art of Recology
description:
September 1 - December 11, 2026

Reclaimed: The Art of Recology presents a survey of 33 artists who were selected to participate in Recology’s Artist-in-Residence program, which began in 1990. Armed with safety gear and a shopping cart, each of these artists have scavenging privileges in the Public Reuse and Recycling Area—what most artists refer to as “The Big Store”—to recycle and reclaim the discarded waste as imagined art objects. Through introspective, playful, and highly original explorations, the artists reveal the hidden stories our rubbish tells us about our complex relationship with the world, while highlighting the need to create sustainable communities.

This exhibition is curated by Emilee Enders. The exhibition tour is organized by Bedford Gallery at the Lesher Center for the Arts, Walnut Creek, CA.

title: Space and the Sacred: Letterio Calapai's Prints
description:
August 25 - December 11, 2026

Between the 1940s and his death in 1993, the printmaker Letterio Calapai produced dozens of works about outer space and Catholic subjects. This exhibition examines how his art transformed as these subjects evolved during his lifetime and reveals how one man understood the changing world around him.

This exhibition was curated by Julia Neufeld G’23 G’24. We gratefully acknowledge the Dryer Family Foundation for supporting this project.

title: The Promise of Public Service Exhibit
description:
The Maxwell School will be the inaugural host of the traveling exhibit “The Promise of Public Service” curated by the National Academy of Public Administration and showcasing public servants at all levels from across America, past and present.

The traveling exhibit is part of the Academy’s yearlong “Celebration of the American Public Servant,” dedicated to strengthening American democracy and public service as we honor the nation’s 250th anniversary.

The full exhibit was showcased at the Library of Congress during the Celebration of the American Public Servant 250 Gala in June, with the traveling exhibit on display in the Maxwell Hall foyer through the fall semester.

title: Talking to Our Tech
description:
“Talking to Our Tech” presents works by students in Media Art and Critique (CRS 360) exploring the intersections of contemporary art, artificial intelligence and new media practices. Bringing together students with varied levels of experience in media arts and technology, the exhibition reflects a semester of experimentation with computer vision, machine listening and image generation techniques. 

At the center of this exhibition is a conversation between the maker and the machine and between the artwork and the viewer. These exchanges invite us to consider how technology participates in creative processes, influences mediation and rewires our relationship to images and information. They reveal the possibilities, complications and unexpected discoveries that emerge when we learn to talk to our tech. 

On View: Friday, Nov. 20, 2026 - Friday, Jan. 15, 2027
Reception: Friday, Dec. 4, from 5:30 – 7:30 p.m.

description:
September 1 - December 11, 2026

Reclaimed: The Art of Recology presents a survey of 33 artists who were selected to participate in Recology’s Artist-in-Residence program, which began in 1990. Armed with safety gear and a shopping cart, each of these artists have scavenging privileges in the Public Reuse and Recycling Area—what most artists refer to as “The Big Store”—to recycle and reclaim the discarded waste as imagined art objects. Through introspective, playful, and highly original explorations, the artists reveal the hidden stories our rubbish tells us about our complex relationship with the world, while highlighting the need to create sustainable communities.

This exhibition is curated by Emilee Enders. The exhibition tour is organized by Bedford Gallery at the Lesher Center for the Arts, Walnut Creek, CA.

title: Space and the Sacred: Letterio Calapai's Prints
description:
August 25 - December 11, 2026

Between the 1940s and his death in 1993, the printmaker Letterio Calapai produced dozens of works about outer space and Catholic subjects. This exhibition examines how his art transformed as these subjects evolved during his lifetime and reveals how one man understood the changing world around him.

This exhibition was curated by Julia Neufeld G’23 G’24. We gratefully acknowledge the Dryer Family Foundation for supporting this project.

title: The Promise of Public Service Exhibit
description:
The Maxwell School will be the inaugural host of the traveling exhibit “The Promise of Public Service” curated by the National Academy of Public Administration and showcasing public servants at all levels from across America, past and present.

The traveling exhibit is part of the Academy’s yearlong “Celebration of the American Public Servant,” dedicated to strengthening American democracy and public service as we honor the nation’s 250th anniversary.

The full exhibit was showcased at the Library of Congress during the Celebration of the American Public Servant 250 Gala in June, with the traveling exhibit on display in the Maxwell Hall foyer through the fall semester.

title: Sunday Catholic Mass
description:
The SU / SUNY ESF Catholic Campus ministry at the SU Catholic Center offers a rich, vibrant ministry. Our mission is to build a strong community that is completely accepting, inclusive, and bound together, regardless of race, ethnicity, or sexual orientation, by God’s universal love. We demonstrate that love through the celebration of the sacraments, small faith-sharing groups, fellowship, volunteer service, music, and social action. 

We seek with all that we do to provide a welcoming, fun, and loving place for people to express their faith, to know that they are not alone and to discover the love that Jesus has for them. 

Our events, which occur at the Catholic Center (110 Walnut Place, across from the Whitman School of Management) unless otherwise indicated, are open to all. 

Also, the Catholic Center has study spaces (library and Great Room) and prayer spaces that could serve as an oasis for quiet meditation, focusing on mindfulness and centering on the Lord. 

For more information, please check Hendricks Chapel’s Roman Catholic Chaplaincy web page.
